text:

Crime shows and jurrors by Randy A. Waterson from American Prison Writing Archive Palantir’s Chief Defends His Company’s Work With ICE by Michael J. de la Merced from New York Times - Dec 3 2025

news and media’s emphasis on violent crime feeds into the “danger imperative” mentioned in the reading, referring to the cultural frame officers are socialized into in which they may face lethal violence at a moment’s notice
Palantir CEO saying he doesn’t want to surveil innocent Americans but “completely” supports efforts to surveil America’s adversaries, and the concept of “function creep”

title: Dragnet Surveillance
text:
Reading

Dragnet surveillance or “the collection and analysis of information on everyone, rather than only people under suspicion” on an unprecedented scale
Through tagging and generating links among previously separate data points, entirely new searches can be performed almost instantly
one of the most transformative features of the big data landscape: the creep of criminal justice surveillance into other, non–criminal justice institutions
Alert-base systems shift the relational structure of surveillance
Decrease in human mediation
In auditable big data systems, queries are serving as quantified proxies for suspiciousness.

title: Dragnet Surveillance
text:
Main Points
“Using a series of data points to reconstruct an individual’s intentions and behaviors (whether incriminating or exculpatory) rests on the assumption of an infallible state, or the assumption that law enforcement will draw a correct conclusion. And, as the analyst above implied, you are not able to consent—or refuse consent—to the collection of your data at each point.” (86)

title: Dragnet Surveillance
text:
Questions?
“High-frequency data collection makes alert-based systems possible, and that carries enormous implications for the relational structure of surveillance.” (73)

How do alert systems change the relational structure of surveillance?
How could changing structures of surveillance impact police accountability and the burden of responsibility?

Brayne says that “even dragnet surveillance serves to reinscribe inequality” (87)

How does the ability to exercise agency or refuse consent to surveillance map onto societal inequalities?
How, if at all, has this chapter influenced your perception of your own digital trail?

section: How to do a code review
text:
How to do a code review
Lots of advice about how to do a review
Reviews should feel:

positive (safe, supportive, growth-driven)
useful (constructive feedback, technical knowledge exchange)
actionable (specific critiques -> specific fixes)
time-constrained (short enough that you are willing to do it again)

title: Code Review / Peer Review + Upgrading our Visualizations
text:
Positive


Reviewer

Look for and say nice things
Focus on the code and not the person
No fawning, no fighting


Reviewee

Believe the compliments
Don’t fix what’s working
No fawning, no fighting

title: Code Review / Peer Review + Upgrading our Visualizations
text:
Useful


Reviewer

Provide extra context / rationale
Assume the best


Reviewee

Follow-up on any information received
Assume the best
Note when you’re repeating mistakes

title: Code Review / Peer Review + Upgrading our Visualizations
text:
Actionable


Reviewer

Focus on what dev can control
Identify specific changes
Identify specific outcomes


Reviewee

Literally fix the specifics
Ask for clarification (!!)
Check: does this match the outcomes?

title: Code Review / Peer Review + Upgrading our Visualizations
text:
Time-constrained


Reviewer

No need to point out same error over and over
Don’t demand perfection
Follow-up later if it gets weird


Reviewee

Check code for same problem throughout
Don’t ruminate
Fix and move on!

title: Code Review / Peer Review + Upgrading our Visualizations
text:
Importance
A good visualization shouldn’t be a puzzle. It should help the audience visually see the finding
It should be…
- Readable: title, labels, scales, text should be concise and use audience-friendly terminology
- Accurate: data should be represented honestly
- Purposeful: should answer some question and/or directly relate to the overall topic
- Focused: should highlight the important stuff, don’t overdo it with the fun design things

title: Code Review / Peer Review + Upgrading our Visualizations
text:
Types of Plots
Bar charts, scatterplots, histograms, line plots, etc. are GREAT plots but what about the the slightly more unique ones?

Sankey Diagram: shows flows between categories or stages; the width of each flow represents its magnitude; plotly
Chlorepleth Map: shows geographic variation using shaded regions; plotly express
Network Graph: shows connections and relationships between entities; #linearalgebra #nodes #edges; pyvis or networkx
Heatmap: shows patterns across two categorical or ordered dimensions using color; can include a temporal element; seaborn or plotly express

*Helpful Packages for Maps: ‘geopandas’ (handles geometric shape files), ‘geopy.geocoders import Nominatim’ (OSM geocoding)

title: Code Review / Peer Review + Upgrading our Visualizations
text:
How to make it pretty
Adjust:
alpha | Transparency (0 = invisible, 1 = opaque) | Overlapping points; dense scatterplots |
linewidth | Line thickness | Emphasize a trend line; de-emphasize gridlines |
s | Marker size in Matplotlib scatterplots | Make points visible without overwhelming the figure |
edgecolor | Marker outline | Separate overlapping points or improve contrast |
figsize | Figure dimensions | Make labels readable and match the final slide/page |
color / hue | Color or group mapping | Distinguish a small number of meaningful groups |
bins | Histogram bin count | Explore distribution shape; check whether conclusions are robust |
. . . The list goes on * Use ‘?’ and ‘help()’ to see all the possible properties of a function!

title: Code Review / Peer Review + Upgrading our Visualizations
text:
Color and accessiblity

Use color to encode something meaningful (such as categorical variable), not just to decorate
Use a small, consistent palette; too many colors make comparisons harder
Don’t rely on color alone—use labels, marker shapes, line styles, etc.
Make the most important element visually prominent; keep gridlines and borders subtle

ACCESSIBILITY: is the figure still understandable in grayscale or for someone who may be color-blind?

title: Code Review / Peer Review + Upgrading our Visualizations
text:
Creating Multiple Plots
-Subplot(plt.subplot) lets you display multiple plots in a single figure window
-Useful when comparing several datasets or parameters side by side
-Common use cases: for comparisons, different variable combinations, model results, control vs. treatment groups

title: Code Review / Peer Review + Upgrading our Visualizations
text:
Annotating Plots

Annotations (plt.annotate) help highlight important points or trends directly on your plot
Makes your visualization easier to interpret and more informative
Can add text, arrows, or other marks to draw attention to specific data
Useful for pointing out outliers, maxima/minima, or noteworthy feature *Keep in Mind: Too many annotations can clutter the chart!

title: Code Review / Peer Review + Upgrading our Visualizations
text:
Adjust Text/Annotation

When adding text labels to crowded scatter plots, labels often overlap and become unreadable
The “adjustText” automatically moves text labels to minimize overlap
Makes plots more readable without lots of manual adjusting

title: Code Review / Peer Review + Upgrading our Visualizations
text:
Identifying Misleading Visualizations
Common Mistakes to Avoid

Broken axis
– Starting y-axis above zero exaggerates minor differences
Cherry-picking/selective statistics
– Hiding parts of the data or focusing only on extremes
Axis manipulation/Misleading Scales
–Stretching or compressing axes to make a trend look stronger/weaker
Unlabeled axes/confusing units

Today’s Agenda

1-2 data visualizations and 1-2 paragraphs of writing are DUE Wednesday
Rae’s our discussion leader!

title: Carceral centralization and expansion
text:
Related Events

ICE ankle monitors in Springfield , Ohio
An Ankle Monitor Gives a False Taste of Freedom

Relevance?
The reading describes electronic ankle monitors as one way that the carceral apparatus extends its control into public and private life. Jefferson observes that these monitors are another way to micromanage devalued populations while appearing to address issues around prisoners rights and prison overcrowding. In separating urban space into inclusion and exclusion zones, electronic monitoring systems compound/codify existing urban divisions and reinforce geographic notions of criminality.

title: Carceral centralization and expansion
text:
Reading

Urban governments abdicate control to companies and respond to resultant increased wealth inequality by criminalizing poverty
Tech/tech-enabled companies fuel and capitalized on this inequality, building tools that both centralized and decentralized carceral control
Beyond prisons, technology has become incorporated into the judicial system, further marginalizing devalued peoples
Ultimately, creates a carceral system akin to a factory, where control, speed, and cost-effectiveness predominate
Altogether, the “barbarity” of the system is veiled by a combination of concerns over public-safety, intellectual property laws, and the social-scientific research apparatus

title: Carceral centralization and expansion
text:
Main Points

Prisons have always been designed to micromanage certain populations (& the emergence of technology only made this easier and more expansive)
Corporations seek/build new avenues of revenue to stave off stagnation; they aren’t only complicit in the implementation of carceral tech, but actively shape society’s hunger for it
This effects more than just incarcerated individuals – public space is increasingly under the influence of the carceral apparatus

title: Carceral centralization and expansion
text:
Questions!

Jefferson notes that there is a “scientific veil” that “conceals the barbarity” of the current carceral system, citing examples of social science researchers who assist in building risk algorithms, or journals dedicated to criminology and crime science research. What are the benefits of having academia involved in this work? What are the pitfalls? What responsibility do academic researchers have to engage/not engage in this kind of work?
What does Jefferson mean by “disciplinary society”? “Control society”? What are the distinctions they draw between the two and how has the digitization of incarceration caused the two to merge?
How does the use of technology in court cases (particularly algorithms that assign defendants risk scores) undermine the notion of “innocent until proven guilty”? Is there a universe in which predictive technologies coexist with this standard?

title: Data Sources
text:
Children & Criminal Justice System Datasets

Survey of Youths in Custody, 1987 The survey provides detailed information on the characteristics of youths held primarily in secure settings within the juvenile justice system. The data contain information on criminal histories, family situations, drug and alcohol use, and peer group activities. For youths committed for violent acts, data are available on the victims of their crimes and on weapon use
Survey of Youth in Residential Placement (SYRP) 2003 [United States] According to the description, the Survey of Youth in Residential Placement (SYRP) is the only national survey that collects information directly from young people in the juvenile justice system. Developed by the Office of Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention (OJJDP), it uses anonymous interviews to ask youth aged 10 to 20 about their backgrounds, facility conditions, and personal experiences
National Survey of Youth in Custody, 2012 The National Survey of Youth in Custody collects confidential data on sexual assault in juvenile facilities to fulfill requirements of the Prison Rape Elimination Act of 2003. Using private audio computer assisted self interviews, the survey gathers detailed background, perception, and victimization information from thousands of youth across various facilities. These findings help the Bureau of Justice Statistics measure and report on the prevalence of sexual victimization in the juvenile justice system
Compendium of National Juvenile Justice Datasets The links aren’t working but I can guess that these data sets will be of use for my project once I find out how to get to them

Which type of spending is most effective in reducing crime long-term?

title: Research Plan
text:
Personal Motivation
I am studying economics in addition to data science and I’ve thought about the allocation of government resources from an economic lens. I’m curious to use real data to explore how different types of government spending (police spending and social spending) affect crime rates. I am focusing on Washington state because I am from Seattle and I have a basic knowledge of the challenges faced by local police as well as their short- and long-term goals. I also have an understanding of the social issues that take the highest priority in the state and the state’s existing channels for social support.

title: Research Plan
text:
Broader Relevance
This research matters because the efficient allocation of resources can create better societal outcomes. Police departments across the country receive a large share of municipal funding, but the outcomes of policing don’t necessarily reflect the amount of resources invested. Further, concerns about police violence and misconduct question the effectiveness of police in response to certain types of social issues. Some people have argued that a share of police funding should be redirected to social services such as cash assistance programs, housing, education, and health services. Analyzing the allocation of police versus social spending in a given county can offer insights into the effectiveness of both types of funding in reducing crime.

title: Research Plan
text:
Example Projects
Link to three example projects that are related to your questions or how you’d like to display your results. List them like so:
Example Project 1: This is a data science project that analyzes crime statistics, demographics, economic indicators, housing, education, and government expenditures to see which factors are the most predictive of crime rates. While this is a statistics-heavy project, it relates to my research questions in that one of the factors it looks at is government expenditures as a predictor of crime rates. This project exemplifies how to navigate the type of data I’ll be working with.
Example Project 2: I really like the visualization in this project that shows reductions in major crime categories through percent change from 2019-2025. The visualization uses red to show an increase and green to show a decrease. It could be cool to look at 2 separate years (or a range of years) and see if there were changes in one category of spending that may correspond to changes in crime.
Example Project 3: I like the way this project separates the shipyards into tiers by risk level. I could work with tiers in my project by separating counties by the per capita crime levels in each (or separate by police spending level, whichever makes the most sense after working with my data).

title: Research Plan
text:
Relevant Literature
Build a ten item literature review for work related to your questions.
As you consider which 10 to include, try to satisfy these criteria:

1 - 2 written by someone on the inside or system impacted
3ish non-academic sources
at least 5 academic sources
no more than 2 items that we’ve discussed in class / from the syllabus

No need to include a full citation. Instead, list them:
Title of Book/Article/Movie: 2-3 sentences about the connection between this work and your research questions. Do not guess at these - do enough research on each item to have definite ways that the material is connected to your research
More Law Enforcement Spending Accompanies Worse, Not Improved Crime-solving: This paper explores police spending in California and finds that police departments are spending more money and solving fewer crimes than they did decades ago. This paper is a good addition to my research as it helps to explain why different levels of police spending are associated with different levels of crime (I’m not sure what my data will show yet but this offers insights that my research will not be answering so including this paper will make my work more comprehensive). – Academic source
Fight violence with more social spending, not more police: This article looks at mutliple instances where social spending successfully decreased crime. One example is Operation Ceasefire, a Boston anti-gang intervention that has decreased murder rates through investment in job skills training, substance abuse counseling, and community education efforts to incentivize the discontinuation of violent activities. This source connects to my research questions as it posits that higher social spending has been associated with lower crime in some situations. – Non-academic source
Policing Studies Measure Benefits To Crime Reduction—But Not Social Costs: This article argues that the social costs of policing are overlooked when people discuss the costs of policing. An example of a social cost stated in the article is a death that results from an unnecessary or extreme use of police force. This is an interesting idea to consider as I discuss the costs of policing alongside the costs of social services. It might not fit perfectly into my research but it definitely addresses an important dimension of “cost” – the social costs. – Non-academic source
Local Government Spending: Policing Versus Social Services: In recent years, US cities have increased the share of their budgets devoted to policing and decreased the share devoted to social services. However, existing research shows that social services can reduce crime in the long-run and police spending may only reduce crime in the short-run. This adds important context to my research, as it’s necessary to consider the long-term effects of government spending. – Academic source
Abolitionist Disjuncture: Reducing Police Violence in Frontline Social Work: This paper is written by a social worker who comments on the reality that social workers sometimes rely on police. The author writes that it’s not as simple as redirecting police funding towards social services to solve social issues. This adds important nuance to my research: we can’t simply conclude that social services need a portion of police funding. The allocation of resources is important, not just the total amount that goes to each sector. – Written by someone on the inside
Defund the Police: Moving Towards an Anti-Carceral Social Work: This article is written by people within the field of social work and argues that social work’s collaboration with police and use of policing constitutes “carceral social work”. Anti-carceral social work includes interventions that decenter police collaborations and focus on community and mutual aid alternatives. This is relevant to my project because it questions traditional methods of social work and thus channels of social spending. – Written by someone on the inside
Washington’s Current Budget: This report is relevant to my research because it breaks down the largest spending areas per capita in state and local expenditures. This report highlights the main areas that the state is targeting with social spending. Public welfare is listed as one of the largest spending areas per capita. – Non-academic source
The Economics of Policing and Public Safety: This article discusses how in the US, the misallocation of police resources in local departments is disproportionately carried by Black and Hispanic people. As I work on my project, it’s important to know that “police spending” is a vague term and there are insights to be gained by looking at where police spending actually goes in each county. – Academic source
Governing Through Police? Housing Market Reliance, Welfare Retrenchment, and Police Budgeting in an Era of Declining Crime: This article discusses how cities address social problems through criminal justice rather than social service capacities. This paper uses similar data to my project, looking at police expenditures between 1992-2010. They find that police expanded partly as a substitute for social service spending. This is relevant to my project as they are looking at police expenditures in addition to social expenditures. – Academic source
Law Enforcement Expenditures and Urban Crime: This paper looks at law enforcement expenditures and crime rates, but specifically expenditure as a determinant of crime. The paper ends with recommendations for resource allocation in light of its findings. This kind of analysis is similar to what I hope to achieve with my project, and this work includes insights into resource allocation that will be key to the analysis I offer in my project. – Academic source

title: Stage 2: Analyzing Data & Scaffolding the Report
text:
I am using three datasets to explore my research questions about spending and crime rates in Washington state counties.

1. How many offenses were logged in each county in 2025?

#dependencies
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from pyprojroot import here

#importing crime dataset
file_path = here('projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/wa_crime_2025.csv')
crime_2025 = pd.read_csv(file_path)

‘crime_2025’ is a dataset containing observations of all offenses logged by every police department in Washington in 2025. Each offense also notes the county corresponding to the department that logged it. I want to sum the number of offenses by county.

crime_2025.columns.tolist()

['ORI',
 'County',
 'Agency',
 'Reference Number',
 'Report Date',
 'Victim',
 'Offense',
 'Location']



#cleaning 

#dropping columns I'm not interested in
crime_2025_clean = crime_2025.drop(columns=["Reference Number", "Victim", "ORI", "Location", "Agency"])

#remove caps lock
crime_2025_clean["County"] = crime_2025_clean["County"].str.title()

#let's get total counts of the number of the offenses in each county in 2025
county_crime_2025 = (crime_2025_clean
    .groupby("County")
    .size()
    .reset_index(name="Total Offenses"))

#there's a county listed in crime called "state agency" I am dropping before joining
county_crime_2025 = county_crime_2025[county_crime_2025["County"] != "State Agency"]

#county_crime_2025 

I choose to drop a column called State Agency, which listed 620 offenses in 2025. After some brief research, I have not been able to determine what State Agency means in this context, but I suspect those may be offenses logged by the Washington State Patrol. Since I am looking at counties specifically, and I do not have spending data for “State Agency”, I choose to drop this column.


2. How many offenses were violent and how many were nonviolent?
Now I’m going to use the ‘crime_2025_clean’ data that lists all offenses to sum by violent and nonviolent crime.

#let's see all of the offenses
crime_2025_clean["Offense"].unique()

#now I'll divide based on FBI UCR definitions of violent & other crime
violent_offenses = [
    "Murder Non Negligent Manslaughter",
    "Rape",
    "Robbery",
    "Aggravated Assault"]

#sorting into violent and other
crime_2025_clean["Crime Type"] = np.where(
    crime_2025_clean["Offense"].isin(violent_offenses),
    "Violent",
    "Other")

#sum types of crime by county
county_crime_type = (crime_2025_clean
    .groupby(["County", "Crime Type"])
    .size()
    .unstack(fill_value=0)
    .reset_index())

#see violent, other, and total all in one df
county_crime_type["Total Offenses"] = (
    county_crime_type["Violent"] +
    county_crime_type["Other"])

#drop 'State Agency' in this df too
county_crime_type = county_crime_type[county_crime_type["County"] != "State Agency"]

#county_crime_type

Deciding how to define “violent crime” in this case was difficult because the offenses listed in this dataset are not specific. I initially wanted to use Washington state law’s definition of a violent offense, but it defines violent crime by degree. For example, rape in the first degree is classified as a violent offense but rape in the second degree is not (Source). My data simply lists ‘Rape’, so I don’t feel that I have the ability use the Washington state legal definition without proper specification. I insteaed defined violent crime using the common crime statistics defintion, which is based on the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting defintion. UCR lists the following as violent offenses (no matter the degree): murder and nonnegligent manslaughter, rape, robbery, and aggravated assault. I choose to label the categories “Violent” and “Other” because crimes that don’t fall into the FBI’s definition of violent crime are not necessarily nonviolent.


3. How much do Washington state counties spend on law enforcement activities? How much do counties spend on social services?

file_lawenf = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/fit_lawenforcementactivities.csv")
fit_lawenforcement = pd.read_csv(file_lawenf, skiprows=6)

file_social = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/fit_socialservices.csv")
fit_social = pd.read_csv(file_social, skiprows=6)


#sort into counties
fit_le_counties = fit_lawenforcement[fit_lawenforcement["Governments/$ Dollars"].str.endswith("County", na=False)]

#39 counties total in WA
#len(fit_le_counties) #output is 39!

#social services data
fit_social_counties = fit_social[fit_social["Governments/$ Dollars"].str.endswith("County", na=False)]

#39 counties total in WA
#len(fit_social_counties) #output is 39!


#cleaning dollar values in the data
fit_le_counties["2025"] = (fit_le_counties["2025"]
    .str.replace("$", "", regex=False)
    .str.replace(",", "", regex=False))
fit_le_counties["2025"] = pd.to_numeric(fit_le_counties["2025"], errors="coerce" ) #some unexpected values in the dollar column, so replacing these with NaN

#cleaning dollar values in the data
fit_social_counties["2025"] = (fit_social_counties["2025"]
    .str.replace("$", "", regex=False)
    .str.replace(",", "", regex=False))
fit_social_counties["2025"] = pd.to_numeric(fit_social_counties["2025"], errors="coerce" ) #some unexpected values in the dollar column, so replacing these with NaN

In the law enforcement spending dataset, law enforcement activities include police operations, traffic policing, administration, crime prevention, training, facilities, and property and evidence room. In the social spending dataset, social services include homeless services, mental health services, public safety services, chemical dependency services, welfare, child services, aging and disability services, veterans services, developmental disability services, and domestic violence services.


4. Do counties spend more on law enforcement activities or social services, on average?

#dropping the columns that I don't want to be present in the eventual joined df
fit_le_counties = fit_le_counties[["Governments/$ Dollars", "2025"]]

fit_social_counties = fit_social_counties[["Governments/$ Dollars", "2025"]]

#these dataframes had a different name for the 'County' column
fit_le_counties = fit_le_counties.rename(columns={
    "Governments/$ Dollars": "County",
    "2025": "Law Enforcement Spending"})

fit_social_counties = fit_social_counties.rename(columns={
    "Governments/$ Dollars": "County",
    "2025": "Social Spending"})

fit_le_counties["County"] = fit_le_counties["County"].str.replace(" County", "", regex=False)

fit_social_counties["County"] = fit_social_counties["County"].str.replace(" County", "", regex=False)

spending = fit_le_counties.merge(fit_social_counties,on="County")

#spending[["Law Enforcement Spending", "Social Spending"]].mean()

In 2025, Washington counties spent an average of $24,960,060 on law enforcement and $65,967,350 on social services.
Now I am joining together the spending data, crime data, and population data.

#population data
file_pop = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/populations.csv")
population = pd.read_csv(file_pop)

#only want county name
population["County"] = population["County"].str.removeprefix(".")
population["County"] = population["County"].str.replace(" County, Washington", "", regex=False)

#just 2025
population = population[["County", "2025"]]
#rename year for clarity in joined df
population = population.rename(columns={"2025": "2025 Population"})

#removing comma and converting from string
population["2025 Population"] = (population["2025 Population"].str.replace(",", "", regex=False))
population["2025 Population"] = pd.to_numeric(population["2025 Population"], errors="coerce" )

#population


#joining crime, spending, and population dfs
county_data_2025 = (fit_le_counties
    .merge(fit_social_counties, on="County", how="outer")
    .merge(county_crime_type, on="County", how="outer")
    .merge(population, on="County", how="outer"))

#county_data_2025
#county_data_2025[county_data_2025.isna().any(axis=1)]

Benton, Chelan, Grant, and Thurston Counties do not have spending data. This is consistent with the data source which explains that “These governments historically report in this dollar category, but have not filed or are currently editing their FY 2025 filing”. These counties will be excluded from analysis for now but hopefully can be included later.


5. Do counties with higher police spending have more offenses?

#dropping the 4 counties with missing spending data
plot = county_data_2025[["Law Enforcement Spending", "Total Offenses"]].dropna()

#making a scatterplot to represent law enforcement spending and total offenses
x = plot["Law Enforcement Spending"]
y = plot["Total Offenses"]
plt.scatter(x, y)

#line of best fit
m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b)

plt.xlabel("Law Enforcement Spending")
plt.ylabel("Total Offenses")
plt.title("Law Enforcement Spending and Total Offenses by Washington State County (2025)")
plt.show()








This scatterplot shows a strong positive relationship between law enforcement spending and total offenses by county. This relationship can be explained by population differences.


6. What’s the crime rate in each Washington state county?

#calculating crime rate (crime rate = numnber of crimes per 100k people)
county_data_2025["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"] = (county_data_2025["Total Offenses"] / county_data_2025["2025 Population"]) * 100000

#county_data_2025

#county_data_2025[["County", "Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]].sort_values("Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)", ascending=False)

Spokane, Garfield, and Benton counties have the highest crime rates. Crime rate captures the number of offenses per 100,000 people, calculated using population and number of total offenses.


7. Do counties with higher crime rates have more law enforcement spending?

#per capita spending
county_data_2025["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"] = (county_data_2025["Law Enforcement Spending"] / county_data_2025["2025 Population"])

county_data_2025["Social Spending Per Capita"] = (county_data_2025["Social Spending"] / county_data_2025["2025 Population"])

#county_data_2025


#scatterplot
plot2 = county_data_2025[["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)", "Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"]].dropna()

x = plot2["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]
y = plot2["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"]

plt.scatter(x, y)

#line of best fit
m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b)

plt.xlabel("Offenses per 100,000 People")
plt.ylabel("Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita")
plt.title("Crime Rate and Law Enforcement Spending by Washington State County (2025)")
plt.show()








There is a weak relationship between crime rates and law enforcement spending per capita. The line of best fit is very slightly negatively sloped. Counties are widely dispersed around the line of best fit, which suggests that counties with higher crime rates do not always spend more per capita on law enforcement. Some counties stand out on this plot as they have high per capita law enforcement spending relative to the rest of the state’s counties.

#correlation coefficient
plot2["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"].corr(plot2["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"])

np.float64(-0.0374176715619598)


The correlation coefficient between crime rate and law enforcement spending per capita is -0.037, meaning there’s essentially no linear relationship between these variables.


Do counties with higher crime rates have more social spending?

#scatterplot
plot3 = county_data_2025[["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)", "Social Spending Per Capita"]].dropna()

x = plot3["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]
y = plot3["Social Spending Per Capita"]

plt.scatter(x, y)

#line of best fit
m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b)

plt.xlabel("Offenses per 100,000 People")
plt.ylabel("Social Spending Per Capita")
plt.title("Crime Rate and Social Spending by Washington State County (2025)")
plt.show()








There is a negative relationship between crime rates and social spending per capita. The line of best fit is negatively sloped. Counties with higher crime rates appear to generally spend less per capita on social services. There is a lot of variation among counties which suggests that crime rates alone do not explain differences in social spending.

#correlation coefficient
plot3["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"].corr(plot3["Social Spending Per Capita"])

np.float64(-0.2258871886700596)


The correlation coefficient between crime rate and law enforcement spending per capita is -0.226, meaning there’s a weak negative realtionship between the variables.


8. Do counties with higher law enforcement spending have lower violent crime rates?

#calculating violent crime rate
county_data_2025["Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"] = (county_data_2025["Violent"] / county_data_2025["2025 Population"]) * 100000


plot4 = county_data_2025[["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita", "Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]].dropna()

x = plot4["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"]
y = plot4["Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]

plt.scatter(x, y)

#line of best fit
m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b)

plt.xlabel("Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita")
plt.ylabel("Violent Offenses per 100,000 People")
plt.title("Law Enforcement Spending and Violent Crime Rate by Washington State County (2025)")
plt.show()








There is a positive relationship between law enforcement spending per capita and violent crime rates, which challenged my assumption that greater spending would be associated with lower violent crime. There is an extreme outlier in the upper right corner of the plot, which appears to be influencing the relationship.

#identify the outlier
county_data_2025.loc[county_data_2025["Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"].idxmax()]

County                                       Garfield
Law Enforcement Spending                    1443127.0
Social Spending                              170017.0
Other                                             122
Violent                                            30
Total Offenses                                    152
2025 Population                                  2416
Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)            6291.390728
Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita        597.320778
Social Spending Per Capita                  70.371275
Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)    1241.721854
Name: 11, dtype: object


The outlier is Garfield County, which happens to be the smallest county (by population) in Washington state. This exposes a limitation in my calculation of crime rate - a county with a small population will get a high crime rate even with very few offenses.


Do counties with higher social spending have lower violent crime rates?

plot5 = county_data_2025[["Social Spending Per Capita", "Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]].dropna()

x = plot5["Social Spending Per Capita"]
y = plot5["Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]

plt.scatter(x, y)

#line of best fit
m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b)

plt.xlabel("Social Spending Per Capita")
plt.ylabel("Violent Offenses per 100,000 People")
plt.title("Social Spending and Violent Crime Rate by Washington State County (2025)")
plt.show()








This plot shows a slightly negative relationship between social spending per capita and violent crime rates, meaning higher social spending per capita is associated with a lower violent crime rate. Once again, Garfield County is a major outlier.

Note










The dataset I am using is The Intersection of Domestic Violence, Race, Ethnicity, and Sex from NYC Open Data. It is stored in my dataset folder. Its associated data dictionary that provides a brief overview of the dataset and how the data are collected is also stored in my dataset folder.



Based on the information provided in this dataset, what role, if any, does both the race and the sex of the suspect and the victim play in the occurrence of domestic violence incident reports in New York City?




I am particularly curious about the race of the victim in these domestic violence reports. I wonder if there is any correlation between the race of the victim and how often/if police file an incident reports.

From the value counts of each unique observation/racial group in this dataset, most of the victims in domestic violence incident reports were Black, with white victims following somewhat closely behind. title: DV Prosecution Research Plan
text:
Personal Motivation
I am researching this topic because I interned with a family lawyer last summer and became interested in several aspects of family law, but particularly in the court proceedings for cases involving domestic violence. Although my lawyer’s work was mainly within civil courts (divorce and child custody), I wanted to specifically examine the role of race in criminal courts and identify whether or not/how instances of intimate partner violence are racialized in legal proceedings, as well as the role racial discrimination plays in interpreting the law regarding what constitutes a criminal act of domestic violence.

title: DV Prosecution Research Plan
text:
Broader Relevance
Given the US criminal legal system’s well-documented precedent for allowing racial bias to justify certain arrests and determine a particular defendant’s sentencing outcomes, I thought it would be really informative to see how that bias plays out when it comes to domestic and, more broadly, gender-based violence. When we consider how race affects perceptions of victimhood similarly to gender for any given crime, but especially domestic violence, I also thought it would be important to add a dimension to my research that explicitly investigates whether or not the race and gender of the abuser and the victim moderate the corresponding police/court response.

title: DV Prosecution Research Plan
text:
Example Projects
Race and Ethnicity Map of New York: I wanted to potentially create a spatial visualization (interactive map) of the police presence or surveillance cameras by neighborhood/region of Manhattan. To make it a trivariate map I’m hoping to find a way to layer the racial demographics of each neighborhood on top of the measure of surveillance. I think this visualization method will most effectively communicate the relationship between my variables.
Dismantle NYC’s Surveillance State: This project is a report and petition for Mayor Mamdani to act on his initiatives to dismantle the various forms of harmful government surveillance in NYC. It includes a lot of helpful background and data points, including the estimated costs of the specified reforms, which I will use to contextualize and broaden my coverage and discussion of the types of racially discriminatory surveillance technologies in NYC policing.
Vital City: Who’s the Guard Really Guarding in US Cities?: I liked how this project highlighted the discrepancy between the cities that Trump’s executive orders involving police force/action targeted and the actual prevalence of crime and violence in those cities. I want to build a similar narrative with my visualizations that highlights the areas of Manhattan that are most heavily surveilled/policed and compare it with the actual rate of violent crime that exists in those areas, with the idea that surveillance technologies are largely based on databases that are far from neutral, but based on arrest data that discriminates against certain racial groups.

title: DV Prosecution Research Plan
text:
Relevant Literature
Build a ten item literature review for work related to your questions.
As you consider which 10 to include, try to satisfy these criteria:

1 - 2 written by someone on the inside or system impacted
3ish non-academic sources
at least 5 academic sources
no more than 2 items that we’ve discussed in class / from the syllabus

No need to include a full citation. Instead, list them:
In the Image of Injustice: A Critical Examination of AI, Surveillance, and Systemic Racism in the United States: This article examines the detrimental impact of AI and its associated technologies in the conducting of crime risk assessments and justifications of surveillance. It covers how these technologies have significant error rates for people of color and are based on algorithms that resulted from a history of racial discrimination and over-policing in communities that are predominantly made up of people of color, thereby challenging the notion that AI and surveillance technologies are neutral/unbiased tools of justice.
Types of AI Surveillance: This article is one of the more “neutral” sources that I am planning to use mostly for background and context about the different types of AI-driven surveillance technologies that governments of various levels and nationalities use. I think this article is a good source of foundational knowledge about the predominant methods of government surveillance and also provides brief discussions of their potential shortcomings/negative impacts, particularly in cases of political fugitives and/or dissidents.
SURVEILLANCE OF BLACK LIVES AS INJURY-IN-FACT: This article is a legal review of the historical precedent for surveilling Black bodies and communities, as well as the legal parameters and justifications for social media surveillance in the digital era. It provides the legal basis for government surveillance measures and the history of racialized surveillance that has evolved into the disproportionate surveillance and targeted policing of Black people’s social media activity.
Fragile Algorithms and Fallible Decision-Makers: Lessons from the Justice System: The authors delve into the various inconsistencies and biases that artificial intelligence predictive algorithms display when used in the criminal justice system. Beyond issues with training the algorithms and addressing conflicts between machine-human assessments, they argue that using it to make important justice decisions like pre-trial release proves to be highly problematic, especially where Black defendants are concerned. I am also interested in this article because it specifically works with data from New York City.
The Dynamics of Racial Residential Segregation: This is a broad historical review of various trends in residential segregation of people of color, particularly Black people, in major American cities and their metropolitan areas. It provides a thorough summary and theorization of the historical development of residential segregation, one of many theories being that it is entrenched by generational poverty and oppressive racialized systems/structures that contribute to stark racial disparities in urban geography. I am interested in using this article as a theoretical basis for my research question as it deals explicitly with racial residential segregation in urban areas.
ICE has spun a massive surveillance web. We talked to people caught in it: NPR covers the widespread use of mass surveillance technologies in ICE raids and stops/detentions, particularly APLR, facial recognition, and social media (Meta). The article is based on interviews with activists/observers and immigrants who were directly detained or stopped by ICE to illuminate the lived ways in which surveillance tools enable ICE and the Trump administration conduct their crackdowns. I will use this work to gain a better understanding of justice-impacted individuals’ encounters with mass surveillance technologies.
Opinion: How Exclusionary Zoning Perpetuates Segregation in New York: This op-ed argues that the history of redlining in New York City has persisted till the modern day as a result of exclusionary zoning, making the city and its metro area the third most segregated region of the country. Calling out the frequently deployed arguments, both historical and modern, about how people of color are a detriment to and unwelcome intrusion on the local economy, the article argues that the city is zoned deliberately to cater to a wealthy, white populace, exacerbated by and directly contributing to gentrification and sky-high housing costs.
Why New York’s ‘Precision Policing’ Raises Civil Rights Concerns: The Marshall Project addresses the use of ‘precision policing’ by the NYPD and the deployment of more police to areas that are deemed to be more high-crime. For example, proponents at the NYPD claim this technology has significantly reduced crime in The Bronx, an argument that contains a notable layer of bias as the Bronx has historically been populated by predominantly Black and brown communities. The article addresses the various civil rights implications attached to these ‘neutral’ surveillance measures that justify increaed police presence and abuses of power in historically marginalized neighborhoods.
Analyzing the First Year of NYC Police Encounter Data from the How Many Stops Act: This source is a brief by the Legal Defense Fund that uses data collected from the How Many Stops Act to highlight the disproportionate policing of Black people in NYC based on the average number of police stops and interactions per person as a function of their race. Additionally, it covers the geographical correlation based on the disproportionate number of encounters with police based on whether or not a given precinct has more Black residents. It argues for more data transparency so that citizens and policymakers are aware of how taxpayer money is put towards perpetuating these racially discriminatory systems.
[Predict and Surveil: Data, Discretion, and the Future of Policing - Ch. 3]: I wanted to include this chapter as part of my relevant literature because it includes the author’s interactions with people who work at Palantir. I found it very illuminative of the general attitude of people who partake in and support mass surveillance of criminal suspects and political dissidents. It also delves into how the technology is used pretty indiscriminately, without much regard for the rights of private citizens and whether or not they are actually culpable for a given crime.

2. What most surprised you about the data you’ve been working with? I was surprised by the racial demographics of the districts that were too big after reallocation. I suspected that I would see elevated Black populations within these districts given the racial nature of mass incarceration. However, while this was true for some districts, many other “too big” districts had similar Black/non-Black ratios as districts that were “too small” after reallocation. Given what I know about Texas , I wonder if the same would hold comparing the Hispanic populations across “big” and “small” districts. (EDIT: I went back and checked this. It does!) More broadly, I’m curious if the racial implications of prison gerrymandering in Texas, California, and New Mexico differ compared to that of other states.
3. What questions do you still have? What would help you answer them? At it’s most base level, I realize that I do not know how successful the reallocation efforts that produced the data I use were. That is, were 100% of the people removed from districts added back to their home districts? (EDIT: I checked this. Yes, essentially)
Likewise, in New York State White, Webley-Brown, and Markovich report that a small number of districts—those containing prisons—lost a large number of individuals, while a large number of districts—from which incarcerated individuals are drawn—each gained only a small number of people. In Texas it appears that this is true; 89 more districts gain individuals compared to the districts that lost individuals. However, I do not know the extent of this gain within each of these districts—though this is an easy question to answer.(EDIT: I checked this as well. The average gain in these districts is 763 or .4% of a single district.)
In addition to the questions above, I have not yet investigated my central research question: “How would the reallocation of incarcerated individuals during the 2020 redistricting cycle impact the distribution of possible legal maps and/or partisan outcomes in Texas.” To answer this I’ll need to run some kind of ensemble model using the Gerrychain package in Python. Howver, there is the another question of which ensemble to use; “flip” ensembles flip the district assignment of a single precinct or census block to produce a new map. However, flip is slow and often fails to generate new maps that differ significantly from the base map. Other, more recent methods include Recombination (ReCom) and Reverse RecCom (Rev ReCom). White et. al use Sequential Monte Carlo, which, like “flip” ensembles, samples uniformly from the world of possible legal maps. However, as DuFord, Duchin, and Solomon point out, assuming a uniform distribution of possible maps is a mistake; ReCom and RevRecom address this uniform sampling issue.
Returning to the demographics of Texas, White et. al. make a good point about NYS being generally representative of other states in key ways; another path for investigation that is potentially relevant is how Texas compares to other states. Does Texas’ size, large Hispanic population, Republican lean, and high incarceration rate make its example less/more relevant to other states? To what extent is it an “extreme case”?
Finally, another unanswered question comes directly from White et. al; they write that they hope to investigate the impact of prison gerrymandering on local-level redistricting in areas with prisons. This is another direction for analysis.
4. What story are you trying to tell with this data?
Ultimately, I am interested in better understanding whether some kind of prisoner reallocation redistricting law would prove to be effective in Texas. That is, would enforced reallocation of prisoners when redistricting actually measurably change the range of possible legal maps and thus partisan outcomes in the state?
Likewise, I’m interested in investigating the impact of new prisons on possible legal maps. To what extent did the building of new prisons in Texas from 2010 to 2020 change the partisan makeup of the state’s legislative chambers?
5. How do you think the insights you’re discovering will be best presented? That is, what kinds of displays might be most effective for the story you’re trying to tell?
I have a few ideas. First, since ensemble methods are used for outlier analysis, histograms are the best way to display the distributions of legal maps/partisan outcomes. Drawing from Duchin’s Data and Democracy Lab’s interactive “Introduction to Ensembles” page, I want to build an interactive tool that lets people “build prisons” on a map and see how the locations they choose shift the maps that are possible.
6. How has your thinking changed since you first wrote your research question? My thinking has largely remained unchanged; my central research question remains the exact same. However, I now have a better understanding of the kinds of supplementary information that may be relevant to that question. I also have a new secondary focus on the impacts of building new prisons. (See Q3)

How do you think you’ll be able to connect your project to others in your research cluster?

House District 95, once adjusted has 10,970.5 more individuals than the ideal district, meaning that many people have been removed from the district’s population via the prison pipeline. On the other hand, district 24 has 14,824.3 fewer people than the ideal, meaning that in actuality, its population is inflated by inmates. All other districts have differences from ideal that are between 10,970 and 14,824.


Since gerrymandering is inherently geographic, I’m curious whether there are geographic patterns to the districts that gain vs. lose population after adjustment. This should be the same thing as finding whether the adjusted districts are too big (i.e., population was gained) or too small (i.e., population was lost).

title: Research Plan
text:
Personal Motivation
I’ve never really thought about where prisons were built, or what they looked like. I want to know about what went into the decisions to build a prison there: was it the local government who decided it? What did the local population think? Does it have anything to do with the proximity to “criminals”? I hope to answer these questions this semester.
This is also a topic I think I will be able to stomach through this semester. My original idea involved media coverage, yet there is no data set for that. Other subjects and topics may dive into darker territory, and I’m not sure if I’ll be able handle researching such dark topics all the time.

title: Research Plan
text:
Broader Relevance
I am wondering if there are any reasons behind building prisons relating to racism, classism, or otherwise. I believe that it is important to examine this aspect of systemic oppression, if it exists, that is not studied very much; I haven’t seen a lot of articles about how prison locations are decided. There is the theory that prisons are built to exploit black and brown prisoners for the benefit of the towns nearby, but I did come across an article that disproved it. So, I am wondering what else factors in that decision.

Relevant Literature
Build a ten item literature review for work related to your questions.
As you consider which 10 to include, try to satisfy these criteria:

1 - 2 written by someone on the inside or system impacted
3ish non-academic sources
at least 5 academic sources
no more than 2 items that we’ve discussed in class / from the syllabus

No need to include a full citation. Instead, list them:
Mapping Prison Proliferation: Region, rurality, race and disadvantage in prison placement: This article discusses the theory that prisons are built in poor white towns in order to exploit the labor of Black and Brown prisoners. I want to research the demographics of the towns and what factors go into the building of prisons, both of which are examined in this article.
“Not in my backyard”: The issues and complexities surrounding prison siting: This article focuses on the different approaches behind choosing the site of a prison, and also gives some attention to the residents’ opinion. Exploring the reasoning behind building a prison is one of my research questions.
Mass Incarceration and the Paradox of Prison Conditions Litigation Schoenfeld The Paradox of Prison Conditions Litigation: The author examines how building into prisons/increasing incarceration can come from rulings that had the opposite intention. This relates to my question of the causes of prison siting.
Are Prisons Obsolete?: She discusses prison distribution in California, and the prison industrial complex chapter has discussion of why prisons are built and by who. I appreciate having a source that discusses prison distribution outside of a data set. This is also one of the few sources I found that discusses why prisons are built
Punishment is Purple: The Political Economy of Prison Building: Given that mass incarceration is a result of the prison boom, this article disproves the notion that republican legislators are the ones responsible for that boom, and it actually is the result of bipartisan voting. This offers a new reasoning behind the decision to build prisons.
Prisons as Panacea or Pariah? The Countervailing Consequences of the Prison Boom on the Political Economy of Rural Towns: The paper shows how economic decline slowed after prisons were built. This reveals possible motivation for building prisons, and supports my initial hypothesis about motivations.
Debunking Four Myths about the Prison Building Boom Supporting Mass Incarceration: Like the title says, this article talks about four myths about the purpose of prisons: prison towns are tiny, white towns; prison building has been led by republicans; prisons don’t benefit the towns they are built in; and mass incarceration is an urban problem. This article also links other scholarly sources that I could use.
New York state seeking proposals to build new prison: This is the statement put out by legislators to build a new prison. A statement from the perspective of the people in power is only one side of the story, but useful for comparing to other motivations
Site of former Stateville Correctional Facility to house new prisons, officials say: Same as above, but in Chicago. It has the same benefits, featuring a main reasoning of new jobs.
Prison Town, USA: A documentary that takes a look at people that live in Susanville, CA (small, rural town in the northeastern part of CA that tries to resuscitate its economy by accepting the construction of a state prison). It follows a mill worker who becomes a correctional officer, a local business owner, and the family of an incarcerated person

title: Treatment of Children in the US Criminal Justice System
text:
This project explores how young people involved in the criminal justice system view themselves, their futures, and their experiences with the system. I am particularly interested in the distinction between being treated as a child and being treated as an adult, and how demographics influence this distinction.
Using survey data from the Pathways to Desistance study, I will examine young people’s educational aspirations, expectations for success, and perceptions of fairness when interacting with police and judges. I want to understand whether young people feel heard and respected by the justice system, how they imagine their futures, and whether their experiences are connected to their expectations for success.
I also plan to interview my father’s friend, who was charged as an adult at 17, to learn how this experience affected his identity and outlook on life. Through all of this, I hope to look beyond how society labels young offenders and better understand their perspectives as young people navigating a system that can shape their futures. I will present my findings through a report that a combination of data visualizations, personal stories, and my outside sources

title: Stage 2 Writing
text:
What data did you think you’d find that you weren’t able to find?

When I first started this project, I was interested in understanding why some children are treated as adults in the criminal justice system. I wanted to investigate how race, age, gender, and offense severity influence whether a young person is charged as an adult. I couldn’t find very detailed datasets on these stats, since children’s personal identifying information is sensitive/restricted. However,instead I’ve found data that can help me understand young people from their own perspectives, which has become a more interesting direction for my project

What most surprised you about the data you’ve been working with?

My biggest suprise so far is from the ??? dataset. For the question on if children felt heard by police, 35.67% of participants said they were allowed to tell none of their story, and the second highest response was participants who said they were allowed to tell all of their story. I thought this was an interesting contrast. It’s the opposite ends of the spectrums and yet top 2 answers. I expected the responses to be more evenly distributed or to lean more heavily toward one side. Instead the results made me wonder why participants reported such different experiences

What questions do you still have? What would help you answer them?

I still have questions about the relationships between young people’s experiences with the justice system and their expectations for their futures. Do participants who feel heard by police and judges have different educational expectations from those who feel ignored? Do participant’s perceptions of fairness change across interviews? Do their educational aspirations and expectations change as they get older? To answer these, I want to explore more of the procedural justice dataset. I also want to investigate whether I can connect responses across datasets using participant identifiers (join). This would allow me to compare participant’s experiences instead of examining each question separately.
I also need to account for missing data. The percentages I calculated for the first and last interviews suggest that educational aspirations and expectations may change over time, but the number of people answering questions also changes. Comparing the same participants across interviews would help me determine whether individual responses change or whether the differences are partly explained by who remains in the study

What story are you trying to tell with this data?

I want to tell a story about what it means to be a young person navigating the criminal justice system while still imagining a future for yourself. I want to move beyond looking at young people only in terms of the crimes they committed and instead explore their identities, goals, expectations, and experiences with authority figures. So far, I’ve found that many participants value educational success, although their expectations do not always match their aspirations. I’ve also found that participants report very different experiences when interacting with police and judges. Some felt they had the opportunity to tell their story, while others felt they were not allowed to explain themselves at all. I don’t yet know whether these experiences are connected, but I want to investigate that possibility. Ultimately, I hope to show that young people involved in the criminal justice system have their own perspectives, ambitions, and understandings of their experiences

How has your thinking changed since you first wrote your research question?

Initially I was thinking of my questions from an outside perspective, like why are children charged as adults? who decides this? But as I explored datasets, I’ve found that it feels more meaningful to focus on children’s personal experiences. I believe my approach offers a more personal and meaningful perspective on juvenile justice. Discussions about young offenders often focus on their crimes, the punishments they deserve, and whether they should be treated as adults. I want to look beyond these outside judgments and better understand the young people themselves. What are their hopes and expectations for the future? Do they feel heard and respected by the justice system? How do they understand their own experiences?

title: Immigration Detention and/or Criminal Justice Outcomes Across Different Immigration Status Before and After COVID-19
text: This project will focus on how the non-citizen incarceration in the United States over the past 26 years (2000–2026). The research aims to find out how incarceration trends have changed and whether these patterns vary based on immigration status. The research will categorize populations into undocumented migrants, legal permanent residents, and asylum seekers. Additionally, this project will evaluate whether the onset of the Covid-19 Pandemic in 2020 served as a factor for significant changes in incarceration rates.

title: Research Plan
text:
Personal Motivation
Growing up in Charlotte, NC I experienced the Charlotte-Mecklenburg School (CMS) system firsthand. Charlotte has a deep rooted history of school desegregation, yet still has evident patterns of racial and economic geographical divide. Throughout the three CMS schools that I attended, it became clear that several inequities existed. I’m interested in exploring the history and data surrounding the extent to which these inequalities exist. I hope to look at the geography of schools and neighborhoods and see the connections that may exist between how young people experience and interact with the criminal legal system. Being able to put statistical meaning to the environment and experiences I grew up with will be eye-opening and motivating.

title: Research Plan
text:
Broader Relevance
The school to prison pipeline is a relatively well known systemic phenomenon. This concept has numerous contributing factors with many interconnected parts. Looking at the relationship that this concept has with geographic and segregated matters is of extreme importance. CMS provides an important case as the district moved from a nationally recognized court-ordered desegregation to substantially greater racial and socioeconomic segregation following changes in school assignment policy. Some research has been done surrounding this issue, but the spatial overlap between school and neighborhood segregation and youth involvement in the criminal legal system is less studied. I hope to bring light to these issues by examining the geographic disparities that continue to persist to this day.

title: Research Plan
text:
Example Projects
Mapping the School to Prison Pipeline in North Carolina, 1972-2016: I thought this project was super interesting as it looks at the relationship between keeping schools safe and keeping students attached to school. The investigated whether different school policies decreased rates of in-school violence in the short term and/or increased rates of conviction/incarceration in the long run. I liked the data sources that they pulled from and some of the statistical analysis that they did.
The Segregation Tracking Project: This project is super super cool! They’ve created a map of the country tracking the segregation that exists. They have map layers for residential segregation, student segregation, regional segregation, and more. This is a big part of what I want to look like so I’m hoping to take inspiration from some of the maps that they’re made and data that they’ve pulled from.
Beyond Black and White: While this project does have some capabilities that no longer work, I thought it was a super helpful timeline of how racial disparities have shifted throughout the education system in CMS. I hope to touch on most if not all of the historical pieces that they included (ex. plessy v. ferfuson, brown v. board, swann v. cms, etc.)

title: Research Plan
text:
Relevant Literature
School Segregation, Educational Attainment and Crime: Evidence from the end of busing in Charlotte-Mecklenburg: This is an important study as it looks at how students living in the same neighborhood but on opposite sides of newly drawn school boundaries have different relationships with the criminal-legal system. I think this study will be pretty foundational to my research as it highlights how a student’s environment can greatly impact the outcomes that they may face later in life.
The School to Prison Pipeline: Long-Run Impacts of School Suspensions on Adult Crime: This paper looks at how school discipline may have an impact on how students are exposed to the criminal legal system from a young age. They look at how things such as high suspension rates may have a bigger impact in the long run. I think this could be really interesting to look at, especially in terms of how the demographics of a school correlates to the type of in school discipline that a school receives.
Cumulative Racial and Ethnic Disparities Along the School-to-Prison Pipeline: This paper takes a similar approach to the above one but focuses more on the racial and ethnic disparities surrounding school suspension and expulsion. It offers lots of theoretical and statistical frameworks which I hope will help guide some of the analyses and data that I use.
What determines school segregation? The crucial role of neighborhood factors: This paper looks at how much of school segregation can be fully attributed to neighborhood characteristics vs school-specific factors. They also look at how this differs amongst urban areas. Since I’m not sure which level of segregation I’m going to look at yet I think this paper will be helpful in making that decision.
The Effects of School Desegregation on Crime: This paper introduces an interesting idea as it looks at the effect that court-ordered school desegregation has on crime. They go on to explain how this also has an impact on the police system as a whole as they notice that police spending decreased years following these court orders. I want to make sure to include this as it shows the impact that it has on the greater community and not just students and schools.
The State of our Children: The statistics in this report are a bit dated, but I think it hints at some super important trends such as adjudications, dispositions, and other juvenile justice issues. It is very detailed with regards to the racial/ethnic breakdown of these topics.
Juvenile Justice in Mecklenburg County: This is a community-oriented report that specifically addresses juvenile justice in Mecklenburg County. It discusses the history of school segregation, school discipline, policy change, and the racial disparities throughout. It has a bunch of cool graphs and staggering statistics that I think will help give me a good basis.
The Impact of Busing in Charlotte: This is a unique format as it’s a collection of oral histories rather than a typed out research study. It includes perspectives from Black and white students who experienced this integration and varying points in time. I think this will be extremely helpful in humanizing the impact of school segregation.
Educational Experiences: Voices of Incarcerated Male Youth & School-to-Prison Pipeline: This brings in a super important perspective as the project is based on interviews of incarcerated young men and their educational experiences. They explain how their school and personal lives played a role in this outcome. Discussing things such as unhealthy environments, substance abuse, and criminal activity.
UNCC Goldmine (oral histories and digital archives): These three oral histories and transcripts all discuss the integration of schools. Two come past students with one being from the CMS superintendent. These first-hand accounts will likely be helpful in characterizing what these times were like and how they compare to now. I was only able to include one link here, but I have two more for the other speakers.

title: Research Plan
text:
Personal Motivation
I am a Black woman from the South and was born and raised there for 18 years, but for the past 4 years, I’ve resided up North and have spent more of the calendar year here than in Georgia. So I’ve had this unique relationship with both geographical locations. As I prepare for my post-graduate future, a big question that stays constant in my mind is, ‘where am I going to live?’ This leads to my motivation. I have heard and experienced many pros and cons of being a Black woman in the South vs the North, but how truly different are they? Does one geographical location truly treat Black individuals better? Now I don’t know if there is a true answer to this question and my research project is not about answering that question broadly. A question that can be representative (but should not be extrapolated as a conclusion) of the larger treatment of Black individuals in the North vs the South is through the legal system.

title: Research Plan
text:
Broader Relevance
This topic is definitely something that affects other Black individuals, that is why there has been so many mass exodus’ from the North and the South respectively. How we are treated in the place we decide to reside in, is a matter of importance to us. I don’t think this is a revolutionary research question and there is research, literature, and pop culture references to the concept, but I want to come at it from a place of understanding why. I have spent 4 years listening, talking, and interacting with Northerners and I feel like there’s a disconnect in how they believe Black people are treated in the North vs the South and the reality. I want to examine how Black individuals are mistreated globally and that although there are real differences in treatment, the similarities matter too.

title: Research Plan
text:
Example Projects
Link to three example projects that are related to your questions or how you’d like to display your results. List them like so:
Project 1: https://www.prisonpolicy.org/blog/2023/09/27/updated_race_data/ The inspiration I will be taking from this project is comparing racial disparities by state. I don’t think just looking at imprisonment specifically is the route I want to take for my analysis (I want to focus on the legal system and imprisonment is a part of that legal system, but not the only component). I also want to use a similar data breakdown/comparison when I am defining treatment of Black individuals through comparing it to White people’s treatment.

text:
Relevant Literature
Build a ten item literature review for work related to your questions.
https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/about/glossary/geo-terms.html This is connected to my research because my entire project’s foundation depends on how I will end up defining the two geographical locations. There is no “government official” definition of those two regions for me to use, however the U.S Census does define it. I don’t know if I will be using this definition for my project, but if I do, I will have a good basis for it.
https://www.oah.org/tah/november-4/rethinking-the-role-of-the-courts-in-the-lives-of-black-southerners/ This article is very interesting and connects to my research because it examines the role, relationship, and experience of the legal system regarding Black individuals in the south, but it does not go about just talking about Black voting rights. This is important because I don’t want my research to be narrowed to the “obvious” but instead, painting a holistic picture of how the legal system was shaped and how that affects Black individuals today.
https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1532673X19843714 This article is connected to my research because it is an academic journal about how defining “the south” is more so about political trends and shifts than a geographical location. Although I will not be using a fluid definition of the south, it is important to recognize how regional definitions are not just the states that define them, but there are a lot of political ideologies, values, etc that go into how it’s defined. Because my research is quantitative and I will be using regional definitions, I want my research to at least acknowledge that there’s more to that definition and this journal does a good job of laying that out.
https://www.un.org/en/chronicle/article/racial-discrimination-and-legal-system-recent-lessons-louisiana Although this article was written in 2007, so not as recent, it is still important in general, but also to my research. It’s important to read about real cases of discrimination especially in the legal system and how the environment itself contributes. There is not a law in Louisiana that outwardly says, “discriminate against Black individuals” and then that law not existing in Massachusetts, but the environment of these places contribute to the treatment of Black individuals which is exactly what my research is about.
https://www.vox.com/first-person/2017/10/31/16571238/black-man-deep-south-race This article is not about the legal system, but still details the experience of living in the south vs living somewhere else as Black person. This connects to my research because it’s important to understand the true experiences of Black people who have moved from somewhere that’s considered more “woke” (in his case, the Midwest) to the South, to then understand the structural reasons (such as the legal system) that influence those experiences.
https://lawreview.colorado.edu/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/15.-Higginbotham.pdf This law review essay connects to my research as it talks about the development of racial profiling, which is a data point that I will be analyzing through looking at the difference of traffic stops. This article talks about how racial profiling, as a concept, was used by the LAPD, but was actually introduced by a law in Virginia, a southern state (by my definition), within Hudgins v. Wright. This article definitely helps me understand the systems that shaped the legal system of the south and how that could affect the treatment of Black individuals today.
https://www.crmvet.org/comm/25coresn.htm This article is really interesting to me because although it is not about the legal system, but an organization, it talks about the differences and similarities to how that organization was run in the Northern states (in this article, the states outside of the confederacy) and the South (the confederate states). This connects to my research because I want to answer what similarities and differences exist in the legal system. It’s good to also understand how these similarities and differences affect/exist in other systems, like national organizations.
https://www.ussc.gov/research/research-reports/2023-demographic-differences-federal-sentencing This research article is extremely connected to my research topic as it’s a quantitative study that looks at the demographic differences in federal sentencing. Federal sentencing is a data point that I want to examine because federal laws are the same throughout the country. This article confirms that Black and Hispanic males get sentenced more often than their white counterparts, but is there a geographical divide/difference? That is what I want my research to answer.
https://static1.squarespace.com/static/631b1bc54d4b3d277179851d/t/646cf9674e16115e6ddef152/1684863335171/Eason_Mapping+prison+proliferation.pdf This article is from my research cluster. When I was thinking about examining the differences in how Black individuals are treated within the legal system in the North v South, prison geography did not immediately come to mind, but after talking with my group and reading some of their literature, I realized that there could be a place for that in my own research question. There could be geographical differences in where prisons are built which could influence the regional similarities or differences in how Black individuals are treated within the legal space.
https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/prison-gerrymandering-distorts-representation Also did not think of looking at prison gerrymandering to help answer my question until the research clusters. This paper talks about prison gerrymandering and how when we count incarcerated people at the prisons (which are typically built in rural, white areas) instead of their home address distorts the legislative population. This is connected to my research question because this can help address what systems help shape the different experiences Black individuals face within the legal system as well as what systems are still in place today.
