import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

# 1. Ensure V14 (year) is numeric

Okay, we’re cooking - we can see that execution by hanging was most popular in the late 1800s/early 1900s, and was replaced by electrocution, which itself spiked in popularity in the 1950s.

import pandas as pd

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()












import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Create a normalized crosstab (normalize='index' means each row adds up to 1.0)

This doesn’t really tell us anything - this also makes sense. Given the LONG coverage of this dataset.

After this calculation, I have found out that the national average percentage of the state population being immigrants is roughly 10.41%. Referring back to the top five states, all five of them had an immigrant share of total state population above 10.41%, with California being almost tripple with a share of 27.6%. Texas has a share of 23.1% which is over double the average. I do not believe this is a coincidence espceially since a common place to find work for undocumented people is the parking lots of The Home Depot and Lowe’s. People will crowd around and wait for people to come pick up supplies and ask if they have any work they need done. I will be exploring this further in this next stage.

title: Flock Camera Usage for ICE Detainment
text:
I have chosen to focus my project on the use of Flock cameras in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detainment. Flock cameras are are an AI powered national surveilance system. There were very little safeguards initially, with police departments having almost unlimited access to a nationwide database of every person and vehicle recorded. Following some backlash, Flock has instilled some more protections but not enough to make the general public feel safe. In the last two years, Flock cameras have sprung up all over the country. Initially they were advertised as a tool to find stolen cars and missing children. My research will focus on how the Flock system has been abused to find and detain people ICE suspects to be illegal immigrants. Flock has stated they do not have a partnership with ICE however the placement of concentration of cameras tells a different story. I will be exploring the top five states with the msot Flock cameras, but ultimately focusing my attention to California which has the largest number of Flock cameras, as well as the largest number of recorded immigrants.

title: Research Cluster
text:
Our research cluster is connected under the umbrella of government intervention. The decisions of local, state, and federal governments have a huge impact on the lives of civilians and prisoners alike. Leah is focusing on how the government is surveilling, or in some cases choosing not to surveil the citizens while Julia is focused on how the government is choosing to spend money. Leah’s research project is based on Flock camera usage within the state of Massachusetts by county, which counties are for or against and how Flock is being used within the police force. Julia’s research project is exploring the allocation of government spending by county in Washington state, and its effect on crime statistics.
We plan on using the cluster to lean on each other when we are struggling with certain aspects of our projects and compare the data we are exploring. We will provide each other with different resources if we find a particular website that offers lots of data. Since both of the projects are looking at the government responses and decision making, we can help each other find supporting data and research opportunities. We are looking at two sides of the same coin with the government. Julia is looking at government spending while Leah is looking at actual legislative response. This type of partnership will help fill in the gaps of each other’s research to create a bigger picture.
Our topics also build off of each other. Governments that choose to use the Flock system are spending money on surveillance, which indicates they are allocating funds to that particular project. We will be able to show which counties are allocating their funds to increase surveillance while which are choosing to use different systems of policing. New technologies and surveillance cost a lot of money so when these new systems are developed, money has to be moved from one place to another. Julia will be able to see where the money is being focused and where it is being taken away from.

title: Assignments
text:
In class work

Class summary sheets / Exit tickets

Why we do it
Reflecting on the material is an important part of working in an application domain. These give you practice responding to ethical/domain-specific questions in the same way you will be asked to do so in your data science career.


What it is
Class summary sheets are handouts that you turn in at the end of some classes answering a question related to that day’s lecture or an aspect of the reading. Some students do not do well speaking in class, others prefer speaking to writing. These sheets give some students a chance to communicate in their strongest medium, and others the opportunity to strenghten their impromptu written communication skills.


How it’s graded
These are graded credit/no credit and cannot be made up if you are absent from class. The only way to get no credit for a sheet that you filled out is if you obviously did not do the reading and obviously are writing answers that are completely irrelevant.
We will have ~25 class meetings this semester, and will only do these on the 12 or 13 seminar days. Full credit for this section is 10 sheets.



Skills review

Why we do it
A data science or computer science career is one in which you’ll be constantly learning new things and explaining them to other members of your team. This gives you a safe way to practice this skill.


What it is
You’ll come to the front of the class and lead us through about a 7-10 minute review of a predetermined skill that we’ve covered previously.


How it’s graded
These are graded credit/no credit and cannot be made up if you are absent from class. The only way to get no credit is if you obviously did not prepare.
We will have ~25 class meetings this semester, and will only do these on the 12 or 13 lab days. Full credit for this is 1 presentation. Depending on the class size, these may be done in pairs, or we may do more than one each lab class.

text:
Leading class discussion

Why we do it
This assignment gives you the opportunity to practice a few important skills: communicating summary information, asking questions about new/complex material, speaking in public (😬), and moderating and facilitating conversations about complex subjects.






Important



You are responsible for signing yourself up to be a class leader. If you cannot attend class that day, you are responsible for switching with another student. Class Leader Schedule




What it is
Leading class discussion involves preparing materials about the day’s topic, summarizing the reading, and then leading class through ~15 minutes of discussion.
When it’s your day to lead, you’ll need to create a branch and make edits to the day’s lecture slides before class. The lecture files are markdown in the lectures folder. You’ll find the appropriate file (week number, class number (for example the Class 1 of Week 2 week2-c1.qmd) . You’ll know where to add your slides by reading the code and finding the comment:
<!-- Discussion Leader: Add your slides here -->
When it’s your turn to lead discussion, you will make these edits:

Create 1 slide with

A link to a piece of inside-written (or other authors who are system-impacted) journalism or reporting about something related to the reading, the coursework, or your particular research project. We do this because it’s important to listen to people who have directly experienced the criminal legal system.

If you’re not sure where to start, try Prison Journalism Project, Prison Writers, The Freedom Archive, American Prison Writing Archive, or works by authors like those associated with the Incarcerated Writers Bureau,

A link to a current news article related to the topic.
1 - 2 sentences about how these are related to the day’s topics

Create 2 slides with an overview of the main points of the reading.
Create 1 slide with discussion questions. Here’s a popular guide for how to ask good discussion questions.
Open a pull request containing JUST these 4 slides (and any associated images that you require which should be stored in lectures/images) and assign it to me by twelve pm the day of the class. Note that the PR must pass all tests, so try not to put it off until the last minute in case tests fail!

if you open a PR with failing tests and don’t fix it yourself, I will fix it and merge before class but/and that will impact your grade on that portion of the assignment

At a certain point (likely different in each class), you’ll come to the front of the room and spend 7-10 minutes discussing the links you found and giving us an overview of the reading.
Then, you’ll have 13-15 minutes to lead discussion with your peers. I won’t participate unless called on. :)

These are graded credit/no credit for each of 7 components:

four complete slides (each credit/no credit)
PR open and building (no credit for an open PR that fails to build - so remember to start early!)
presented slides for 7-10 minutes
facilitated discussion for 13-15 minutes

The research project will have many component parts and will be a project that we scaffold over the course of the semester so that you will have the chance to continue to refine and revise your thinking. In order to follow along with this class (and as a customary practice in industry), it’s your responsibility to make sure that your working environment matches what’s below.






Important

Development: You’ll see me write code, and do all of the work for this course in Positron. 💡 Installation Instructions
Coding Language: You can write code in any language you choose. However, I will only be teaching, troubleshooting, and doing demos in Python. You’ll need to be running Python version 3.14.5. Check your python version with python –-version in the terminal. If you’d like to do your coursework in R, you may be able to get support through the Spinelli Center
Installing packages/libraries/modules: We never install python libraries globally. Instead, we work within python virtual environments. There are many modern virtual environments you can use, but I’ll default to the one that comes with Python: venv. 💡 How venv works
Version control: We use git for version control. You will not be able to complete class assignments, participate in in-class activities, or complete your final if you don’t have git installed on your machine and if you are not comfortable using it. I teach git skills in the terminal. Check that you have git installed by running git --version in the terminal.
Bonus: When you look at my terminal, you’ll notice some bells and whistles that you likely don’t have available. If you’d like them, you can use Oh My Zsh as your shell.

title: Stage 2 Writing
text:
In this file, reflect on what you’ve learned (overall across all 8 or more questions you’ve asked and answered) and how you’d like to complete the project.
Answer at least 5 of the following questions:

What data did you think you’d find that you weren’t able to find? I thought I would be able to find data that tracked the change in incarcerated populations over time, but I wasn’t able to find that in one centralized place. I thought about trying to piece together a dataset, but I was worried about double counting people. Also, the most descriptive data I found was recorded a month-by-month basis, and trying to piece together a dataset spanning 10 or more years, would have been more than I could manage. So, I thought it would be more effective to just look at a recent snapshot.
What most surprised you about the data you’ve been working with? Of course, considering historical inequalities, it makes complete sense that Black people are disproportionately incarcerated, but when looking at the demographic information, it was still a little bit surprising to see that Black people are currently disproportionately incarcerated at a rate almost 3x higher than the overall population of Texas. It’s especially jarring to see that no other population demographic had a similarly completely mismatched percentage in the makeup of prison demographics compared to the overall Texas population.
What questions do you still have? What would help you answer them? I’m still wondering about if there are any state-specific policies that have lead to the current demographic breakdown in Texas prisons. Is there anything about the type of prison facilities that have been built, or specific laws that have dispropotionately impacted certain populations? I’m relatively aware of nation-wide impacts, such as the war on drugs, but I’m curious about state-specific policies. I would likely need to do further research outside of my specific dataset to find out about these potential policies.
What story are you trying to tell with this data?
How do you think the insights you’re discovering will be best presented? That is, what kinds of displays might be most effective for the story you’re trying to tell? I think maybe bar graphs would be straightforward and effective. I could make bar graphs that compare the incarcerated population to the Texas population overall. Maybe also some clearly labeled pie charts to illustrate percentages would also be useful.
How has your thinking changed since you first wrote your research question? I was first trying to conceptualize the project as an exploration of change over time, but my thinking shifted to just looking at a recent snapshot of the Texas prison systems. I think narrowing my focus allowed me to also think about looking specifically for patterns in race and type of offense.
How do you think you’ll be able to connect your project to others in your research cluster?

title: Research Plan
text:
Personal Motivation
I was born and raised in Portland, OR, and after my first year of college, my parents and brother moved to Texas. But since the move happened while I was already in college, I don’t know many people in Texas, and I don’t really spend much time outside my house when I do visit during breaks. Although I haven’t spent much time in Texas myself, or perhaps because of that, I feel like it is important for me to understand the political landscape of the state in which I technically live. Additionally, one of my closest friend’s father used to be incarcerated in Texas, so I would like to generally be more familiar with the landscape of Texas prisons.

title: Research Plan
text:
Broader Relevance
In addition to my personal connection to Texas, I would say Texas is a relatively prominent state in the national political sphere, with Governor Abbott making headlines and prominent companies such as Tesla moving to Texas. Furthermore, Texas has experienced an influx of people moving to the state over the past few years, and it would be interesting to see whether or not the change in the state’s overall population has had any effect on the prison population. Texas has also placed stricter laws on THC products and severely restricted healthcare access to abortion and gender-affirming care, and it would be interesting to contextualize those legislative changes with prison data.

title: Research Plan
text:

title: Research Plan
text:
Relevant Literature
Build a ten item literature review for work related to your questions.
Prison Population Reductions and COVID-19: A Latent Profile Analysis Synthesizing Recent Evidence From the Texas State Prison System: The pandemic had a large impact on every facet of life in the early 2020s. I think to understand changing prison populations within the past 25 years, this paper would help contextualize the impact of COVID-19, especially in terms of related deaths and resulting changing in prison population.
Propertied bodies: race, welfare, and the carceral state the Texas way: This paper approaches the question of incarceration in Texas with an emphasis on structural inequality. The article specifically discusses how shifting demographics and neoliberal conceptions of whiteness contextualize Texas incarceration.
Disentangling Differences in Homicide Incarceration Rates by Immigration Status: A Comparison in Texas: This paper provides helpful context for immigration and incarceration. It discusses the impact immigration status has on homicide incarceration rates, specifically in Texas.
Why Can’t I Get a Clean Food Tray at this Texas Prison?: This article provides important perspective from someone on the inside of a Texas prison. It specifically discusses inequalities within the prison system, and how the experience of prison can greatly differ.
How many people are in prisons in Texas?: This website provides a high-level overview of incarceration rates in Texas. The web page has multiple graphics and interactive visualizations that contain data similar to what I would draw upon for my project.
Families of Victims Who Died From Heat in Prison Fight to Prevent More Deaths: This article shares discusses the conditions inside Texas prisons that have resulted in deaths. It shares perspective from system impacted communities regarding the poor conditions in Texas prisons.
Steeped in a Culture of Violence : Murder, Racial Injustice, and Other Violent Crimes in Texas, 1965-2020: This book examines trends associated with various types of violence within the state as well as social and political responses from 1965 to 2020. This will provide important historical context to my examination that begins at 2000.
Tall walls and high fences : officers and offenders, the Texas prison story / Bob Alexander. Richard K Alford.: This paper provides a more qualitative approach to Texas prisons. It outlines the historical context of Texas prisons from the perspective of former employees.
Federal Census policy breaks Texas’s democracy — state lawmakers can fix it: This article from the Prison Policy Initiative outlines inequalities that exist in the counting of incarcerated people. It describes the ways in which prison gerrymandering disproportionately harms Black inmates.
Texas profile from the Prison Policy Initiative: This article discusses a high level overview of various prison statistics in Texas. It includes discussion about more recent data from Texas prisons.

I am against police officers being able to abuse their power without checks and balances. This example captures my own real, work-in-progress thinking about this dataset. I haven’t gone back and made any revisions. I am writing this page at the same time as I’m asking these questions. What is in this dataset? What kinds of questions might I want to ask as I drill down?






The dataset is Executions in the United States, 1608 - 2002: The Espy File. It is stored in the _data folder, and the entire set of downloaded files from ICPSR is in the folder ICPSR-08451. Below, you’ll see that I’m using inscrutable column names. They are labled in the file projects/demo/_data/ICPSR_08451/DS0001/08451-0001-Codebook.pdf



My initial research question is pretty vague – “Are there trends in the crimes for which people have been executed in the United States?” And if I’m being honest, this isn’t the right question for someone with both my disciplinary background and my technical skillset/interests. I’m more interested in how this dataset is shaped, and what I might learn from the kinds of values I’m seeing in it. (This is a more inductive approach.)




I notice that there is a field that defines the sex of the person. What’s the gender breakdown within this dataset?

title: Research Plan
text:
Personal Motivation
I am a Black woman from the South and was born and raised there for 18 years, but for the past 4 years, I’ve resided up North and have spent more of the calendar year here than in Georgia. So I’ve had this unique relationship with both geographical locations. As I prepare for my post-graduate future, a big question that stays constant in my mind is, ‘where am I going to live?’ This leads to my motivation. I have heard and experienced many pros and cons of being a Black woman in the South vs the North, but how truly different are they? Does one geographical location truly treat Black individuals better? Now I don’t know if there is a true answer to this question and my research project is not about answering that question broadly. A question that can be representative (but should not be extrapolated as a conclusion) of the larger treatment of Black individuals in the North vs the South is through the legal system.

title: Research Plan
text:
Broader Relevance
This topic is definitely something that affects other Black individuals, that is why there has been so many mass exodus’ from the North and the South respectively. How we are treated in the place we decide to reside in, is a matter of importance to us. I don’t think this is a revolutionary research question and there is research, literature, and pop culture references to the concept, but I want to come at it from a place of understanding why. I have spent 4 years listening, talking, and interacting with Northerners and I feel like there’s a disconnect in how they believe Black people are treated in the North vs the South and the reality. I want to examine how Black individuals are mistreated globally and that although there are real differences in treatment, the similarities matter too.

title: Research Plan
text:
Example Projects
Link to three example projects that are related to your questions or how you’d like to display your results. List them like so:
Project 1: https://www.prisonpolicy.org/blog/2023/09/27/updated_race_data/ The inspiration I will be taking from this project is comparing racial disparities by state. I don’t think just looking at imprisonment specifically is the route I want to take for my analysis (I want to focus on the legal system and imprisonment is a part of that legal system, but not the only component). I also want to use a similar data breakdown/comparison when I am defining treatment of Black individuals through comparing it to White people’s treatment.
Project 2: https://openpolicing.stanford.edu/ Inspiration I will be taking from this project is most likely the data itself and maybe similar methodologies. I think looking at how Black individuals are treated in different states even before they officially enter the legal system is a good way to go about answering my research question.
Project 3: https://www.law.berkeley.edu/library/legal-research/black-americans-and-the-law/ What I like about this project is that they’re using categorical data; the history/introduction of these laws. I don’t want just to use quantitative data to answer my question, qualitative data is important too. A lens that I could look through that this project shows is tracing the development of the legal system South and the North through the laws itself. I think that analyzing the laws would be a great foundation to start my analysis.

title: Research Plan
text:
Relevant Literature
Build a ten item literature review for work related to your questions.
https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/about/glossary/geo-terms.html This is connected to my research because my entire project’s foundation depends on how I will end up defining the two geographical locations. There is no “government official” definition of those two regions for me to use, however the U.S Census does define it. I don’t know if I will be using this definition for my project, but if I do, I will have a good basis for it.
https://www.oah.org/tah/november-4/rethinking-the-role-of-the-courts-in-the-lives-of-black-southerners/ This article is very interesting and connects to my research because it examines the role, relationship, and experience of the legal system regarding Black individuals in the south, but it does not go about just talking about Black voting rights. This is important because I don’t want my research to be narrowed to the “obvious” but instead, painting a holistic picture of how the legal system was shaped and how that affects Black individuals today.
https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1532673X19843714 This article is connected to my research because it is an academic journal about how defining “the south” is more so about political trends and shifts than a geographical location. Although I will not be using a fluid definition of the south, it is important to recognize how regional definitions are not just the states that define them, but there are a lot of political ideologies, values, etc that go into how it’s defined. Because my research is quantitative and I will be using regional definitions, I want my research to at least acknowledge that there’s more to that definition and this journal does a good job of laying that out.
https://www.un.org/en/chronicle/article/racial-discrimination-and-legal-system-recent-lessons-louisiana Although this article was written in 2007, so not as recent, it is still important in general, but also to my research. It’s important to read about real cases of discrimination especially in the legal system and how the environment itself contributes. There is not a law in Louisiana that outwardly says, “discriminate against Black individuals” and then that law not existing in Massachusetts, but the environment of these places contribute to the treatment of Black individuals which is exactly what my research is about.
https://www.vox.com/first-person/2017/10/31/16571238/black-man-deep-south-race This article is not about the legal system, but still details the experience of living in the south vs living somewhere else as Black person. This connects to my research because it’s important to understand the true experiences of Black people who have moved from somewhere that’s considered more “woke” (in his case, the Midwest) to the South, to then understand the structural reasons (such as the legal system) that influence those experiences.
https://lawreview.colorado.edu/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/15.-Higginbotham.pdf This law review essay connects to my research as it talks about the development of racial profiling, which is a data point that I will be analyzing through looking at the difference of traffic stops. This article talks about how racial profiling, as a concept, was used by the LAPD, but was actually introduced by a law in Virginia, a southern state (by my definition), within Hudgins v. Wright. This article definitely helps me understand the systems that shaped the legal system of the south and how that could affect the treatment of Black individuals today.
https://www.crmvet.org/comm/25coresn.htm This article is really interesting to me because although it is not about the legal system, but an organization, it talks about the differences and similarities to how that organization was run in the Northern states (in this article, the states outside of the confederacy) and the South (the confederate states). This connects to my research because I want to answer what similarities and differences exist in the legal system. It’s good to also understand how these similarities and differences affect/exist in other systems, like national organizations.
https://www.ussc.gov/research/research-reports/2023-demographic-differences-federal-sentencing This research article is extremely connected to my research topic as it’s a quantitative study that looks at the demographic differences in federal sentencing. Federal sentencing is a data point that I want to examine because federal laws are the same throughout the country. This article confirms that Black and Hispanic males get sentenced more often than their white counterparts, but is there a geographical divide/difference? That is what I want my research to answer.
https://static1.squarespace.com/static/631b1bc54d4b3d277179851d/t/646cf9674e16115e6ddef152/1684863335171/Eason_Mapping+prison+proliferation.pdf This article is from my research cluster. When I was thinking about examining the differences in how Black individuals are treated within the legal system in the North v South, prison geography did not immediately come to mind, but after talking with my group and reading some of their literature, I realized that there could be a place for that in my own research question. There could be geographical differences in where prisons are built which could influence the regional similarities or differences in how Black individuals are treated within the legal space.
https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/prison-gerrymandering-distorts-representation Also did not think of looking at prison gerrymandering to help answer my question until the research clusters. This paper talks about prison gerrymandering and how when we count incarcerated people at the prisons (which are typically built in rural, white areas) instead of their home address distorts the legislative population. This is connected to my research question because this can help address what systems help shape the different experiences Black individuals face within the legal system as well as what systems are still in place today.

What data did you think you’d find that you weren’t able to find?
Going into this assignment I thought I’d be able to find more data relating to juvenile arrests. After combing through lots of different sources, I learned that certain information is kept from the general public in order to support juvenile rehabilitation.
What most surprised you about the data you’ve been working with?
I was most surprised by the extent of racial and socioeconomic disparities in school suspension rates. When looking at the median STS rate for Black students we saw their rate was nearly five times that of white students. Similarilly, economically disadvantages students had more than twice the median ISS and STS rates of non-economically disadvantaged students. I had a suspicion that these pattern’s existed, but seeing the actual statistical values next to them made them much more staggering.
What questions do you still have? What would help you answer them?
Most of the questions I have now relate to the historical information surrounding the why behind suspension rates, demographic breakdowns, and geographic disparities. I want to explore the more qualitative parts of neighborhood characteristics, past/current policy, and how things have changed over time. I also want to see if I can find anything relating to funding info about CMS schools and am also considering comapring the geography of school demographics with the geographical demographics of Mecklenburg county as a whole. These are on my to-do list. While I wish I could look at more data surrounding juvenile arrests I understand that this data is not readily available.
What story are you trying to tell with this data?
I’m trying to show the vast disparities that exist within CMS. Since Mecklenburg County is a relatively diverse area with a long history of segregation and political divide, I really want to dive into how this is felt by the people (specifically young-adults). I hope to identify patterns, raise questions, and show the historical implications that still exist.
How do you think the insights you’re discovering will be best presented? That is, what kinds of displays might be most effective for the story you’re trying to tell?
I think a combination of statistical summaries, maps, and potential visualizations will be most helpful. Comparing things such as median values will clearly communicate the disparities that exist. I also think an interactive map of some sort will be useful in showing the clustering of schools within CMS. I haven’t landed on a visualization that is completely finished but I think I have a few components that I want to combine.
How has your thinking changed since you first wrote your research question?
Since I haven’t been able to obtain data relating to the connection between school discipline and students’ later involvement in the criminal legal system, I decided to shift my focus to one that looks at school-level patterns in disciplinary rates and law enforcement contact. My original research question(s) were quite ambitious, which I’ve now realized. I’m now in the process of narrowing and fine-tuning this direction, so that I can present and answer a data-driven question accurately.

title: Hayden’s Research Project
text:
The goal of this project is to examine how racial and socioeconomic inequalities in school discipline and law enforcement contact vary across Charlotte Mecklenburg Schools (CMS). I’m also looking to explore how these patterns relate to the geographic distribution of schools in Mecklenburg County. I’m interested in how these findings connect to the historical contextualization surrounding school segregations and other inequalities. I will begin by examining the racial and economic breakdown of schools and then examine how suspension rates, law enforcement referrals, and school-related arrests interact with these demographic features. From a geographic lens, I plan to map these demographic differences and connect this to broader historical and institutional systems. While my initial research questions were hoping to consider neighborhood segregation, school boundaries, and juvenile/young-adult involvement in the criminal legal system, after reviewing the data I have access to these factors may be beyond the scope of this project. Ultimately, I hope to identify descriptive patterns specific to Mecklenburg County that reveal a relationship between school demographics, disciplinary practices, law enforcement contact, and geography, while also contacting these patterns to larger systems.

text:
How is perhaps Immigrants being treated differently from US born citizen in the criminal justice system?
Is Covid-19 Pandemic one of the factor that fostered a bigger difference?
Specifically during criminal court and/or incarceration how are noncitizens treated differently.

title: Research Plan
text:
Personal Motivation
Being an international student, I’m not that familiar with the Criminal Justice System in the US. From news I’ve seen, I acknowledge these differences exist, but I don’t know how these differences actually plays out on people/this population of people.

title: Research Plan
text:
Broader Relevance
When the same charge can mean probation for a citizen but months in detention for an immigrant, it is against the basic promise that the law treats everyone alike. I want to know whether that gap is real and, if it is, whether the Covid-19 Pandemic made it even wider. The answer matters to anyone who cares about family stability and the way we define belonging in the U.S.. If immigration status quietly shapes bail, sentencing, or release decisions, researching on it is the first step to promote fairness.

title: Research Plan
text:
Example Projects
Detention Mapping Project: First, this interactive map project and my ideal research would both focus on the situation of non-citizens/immigrants within the U.S. criminal justice/detention systems. The Detention Mapping Project categorize information by theme and visualize them by temporal and geographical dimensions. This inspire me on how I organizes multiple measures over time.
The Marshall Project - Immigration: The Marshall Project’s immigration section combine hard data with individual stories. Many of their pieces trace the arc from a local criminal charge to ICE custody, mirroring my focus on how immigration status can stretch a single case into extra time behind bars.
Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC): The TRAC shows how raw FOIA files can be transformed into transparent, time-series data. Their public dashboards also let readers move from headline numbers down to the underlying records.

title: Research Plan
text:
Relevant Literature

Noncitizen Justice: The Criminal Case Processing of Non-US Citizens in Texas and California This article uses court records from Texas and California (2005-2019) to show how charging, pleabargains, and sentence lengths differ for immigrants (undocumented people, lawful permanent residents, and visa holders). The model used in the article give me an overview of people’s status in two of the very highly populated states.
Law-Abiding Immigrants: The Incarceration Gap between Immigrants and the US-Born, 1870–2020

The source documented immigrant–native incarceration gaps and include detailed figures for 2000-2020,using census micro-data and prison rosters. The data for the 2000–2020 period overlaps with my timeframe I’m aiming for. I see it as a research I can try to build apon.

Immigrants are not criminals: Respectability, immigration reform, and hyperincarceration he article argues that the “good immigrant / bad immigrant” storyline has steered lawmakers toward policies that cage non-citizens far more often than the actual crime data would warrant. That lens helps me read my own numbers. If my results show longer sentences or more pre-trial jail time for non-citizens, this piece offers an explanation (stigma and policy design).
TRAC Immigration This source provides annual data on ICE detention figures, lengths of stay, and transfer sources from the year 2000 onwards. I can connect this with state prison or federal sentencing data to estimate exactly how much longer non-citizens were detained due to the “criminal-to-immigration” pipeline.
A day in the life of a 19-year-old in ICE detention: ‘I feel that this nightmare is not going to end’ The report tells an undocumented minor who was transferred from a county detention facility to ICE custody, only to face indefinite detention. The article clearly explains the process of “dual detention” for the same case. It inspire me to consider the issues of transparency regarding detention reviews in the post-pandemic era.
Letters From Detention The website collects hundreds of handwritten letters from detained immigrants, covering topics such as pending transfers, denied bail, and the hardships faced by their families. These letters make me understand more the lived experiences behind the “extra days of detention” figures in the data tables.
Citizenship and Punishment: The Salience of National Membership in U.S. Criminal Courts The author calculated that non-citizens receive sentences averaging 4–11% longer than those of citizens. It concluded that ‘Noncitizens face harsher U.S. prison sentences compared to citizens’. This article presents standard control variables and models, I can maybe try adopt this framework.
Disparities in the Pretrial Process: Race, Ethnicity, and Citizenship Research shows that non-citizens face greater difficulty obtaining bail and endure longer periods awaiting trial, meaning the disparity begins to accumulate well before sentencing. This makes me realize that the disadvantage is not merely compounded at the sentencing stage. It let me think more about my analysis of total detention duration.
Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens by United States Sentencing Commission This show tells me, officially, exactly how many non-citizens were sentenced by federal courts, which offenses were most common, and the average sentence lengths. I can compare it against the trends I’ve mapped out for the 2000–2026 period to check for any discrepancies.
What Happens if an Undocumented Immigrant is Facing a DUI Charge? The article breaks down the entire process—from an undocumented person’s arrest for drunk driving to the issuance of an ICE detainer—into clear steps, while also highlighting specific pain points such as exorbitant bail and prolonged detention. It gave me insight into the practical realities of how immigration status affects the handling of misdemeanor cases.

title: Research Plan
text:
Phase 2 Research Question

How do children who were put in the criminal justice system view themselves, their futures, and their relationship with the justice system?

title: Research Plan
text:
Personal Motivation
I’m interested in this topic because it’s questions that have come up to me as I’ve seen the way children are treated in the media when it comes to ‘crime’ commiting. In particular, I’ve noticed that young school shooters are often treated on social media as derserving of harsh, adult-like sentences. Just recently, I saw the Apalachee High School school shooter who was only 16, sentenced to life without parole. My dad’s best friend was charged as an adult at 17 to almost 7 years for a crime he commited, and it makes me wonder why he was treated as so. Was it because of the crime he committed? Or because he was a black teenager? Why was his sentence so long if it was his first offense? This made me want to investigate this discrepancy we often see today in how children are treated in the criminal justice system.

title: Research Plan
text:
Broader Relevance
Demographic disparaties are well studied in the the juvinile system, so that isn’t understudied. But I believe the understudied side is understanding the experience of children who are charged as adults. There isn’t many statistics or studies on this. Through my project combined with my dad’s friend’s personal story, I believe I can tell an insightful story of children’s experiences with the criminal justice system

title: Research Plan
text:
Example Projects
Youth in Adult Courts, Jails, and Prisons: I really like the layout of this project. It gives a brief summary on top and starts with the history of youth in adult courts/jails/prisons. Then leads into the main points with good use of data visualizations.
Why The Super Rich Are Inevitable: I really like the scroll feature and the fact they started their report with a personal story. I’m really inspired by how visual it is. While it’s discussing a serious topic, it’s still creative and attention-catching
These numbers show that black and white people live in two different Americas: I really like the balance of a little text, followed by a graphic/visualization, little text, graphic/visualization, and so on. I think I’ll try making my report a good balance of text and visualizations.

title: Research Plan
text:
Relevant Literature
TBD Interview Answers: I don’t have this data yet, but I plan to ask my father’s friend about his experience being charged as an adult and how that has impacted his life, his sense of identity, etc, and use that in my research. This can help in my third research questions focusing on how children put into the criminal justice system view themselves
I Was A Child In An Adult Prison System. Now I Fight For Those, Like Me, Who Deserve A Brighter Future When They’re Released: Catherine Jones was charged with second degree murder at 13 and spent over 16 years in Florida’s adult prison system. She describes how she was instantly relabeled a “super predator” and “killer” rather than a child, which speaks to Research Question 1 (where the line between child and adult is drawn) and how the public frames young offenders. She also says that her abuse went unheeded by adults she told, that prison programming was withheld from people serving long sentences, and that employers turned her away after release, all of which show the impacts of being charged to long sentences as a child (question 3).
Children Charged as Adults in Justice System Have Overwhelming Histories of Trauma, Researchers Find: The Imprint interview (Sara Tiano’s Q&A with researcher Aiden Lesley) summarizes a Human Rights for Kids survey of more than 2,200 people incarcerated for crimes committed as minors, finding that 94 percent experienced multiple childhood traumas and that this history was considered in court in only about 10 percent of cases. That speaks to Question 1, because it shows the “adult” label is applied without weighing the developmental and trauma factors that distinguish children. This interview also gives some insight into some of the harsh experiences children face once in prison (abuse risk, solitary confinement, etc)
Youth Confinement: The Whole Pie 2025: Using 2022 juvenile court data, the report finds that Black youth were 37% of delinquency cases but 59% of judicial transfers to adult court, while white youth were 43% of cases and 26% of transfers, and that the disproportion has worsened since 2005. It also cites Florida data showing prosecutors direct-file Black boys at seven times the rate of white or Latino boys, and its footnotes speak to Question 1: four states (Georgia, Louisiana, Texas, and Wisconsin) automatically prosecute 17 year olds as adults, and 22 states plus DC had at least one transfer provision with no minimum age as of 2019. The report also discusses adultification and the “super predator” myth, which ties back to my potential question 4
Most children charged as adults in Washington are youth of color: Henshaw reports that in 2023, 83% of Washington children charged as adults were not white, and that disparities appear both where state law mandates adult charging and where prosecutors have discretion. A 2024 University of Washington report found that of 28 cases where a white child was charged with first or second degree assault with a deadly weapon, none went to adult court, compared with 28% of similar cases involving Black and Latino youth. The article also ties this to adultification, with lawmakers pointing to language in court documents. This all touches on my research questions 1,2, and 4
A New Juvenile Justice System: Total Reform for a Broken System: Henning argues that prosecutors, who hold the most discretion over whether a youth is charged, are influenced by racial stereotypes about maturity and dangerousness. She cites studies showing that race shifts how culpable, mature, and deserving of harsh punishment a young offender is judged to be, even though self report data show adolescents of all races engage in similar risk taking. This connects to my questions 1 and 2 of who draws this line and the factors that influence whether a child is treated as an adult
Off Balance: Youth, Race & Crime in the News: This is a study focused on answering the questions: (1) does news coverage reflect actual crime trends, (2) how does news coverage depict minorities and crime, and (3) does news coverage disproportionately depict youth of color as perpetrators of crime? This connects to my research question 2 about factors that influence how children are treated in the criminal justice system, as well as my potential question 4 about how media/public narratives about young offenders differ by race and type of crime
Girlhood Interrupted: The Erasure of Black Girls’ Childhood: the report finds that adults in a survey saw Black girls as more adult-like and less in need of protection and nurturing than white girls, starting as early as age 5, and it links that “adultification” to harsher discipline in schools and the juvenile system. That speaks to where the line between child and adult gets drawn, and it covers both race and gender, two of the factors in my research question 2. This also touches on my potential 4th question
The Essence of Innocence: Consequences of Dehumanizing Black Children: Goff and colleagues ran a series of studies showing that Black boys are seen as older and less innocent than white boys, and that this perception carried over to how much culpability people assigned them. The authors also found that police officers who held dehumanizing associations toward Black people were more likely to have used force against Black children in custody. This strongly connects to my second research question as well as my potential 4th question
Race and the Fragility of the Legal Distinction between Juveniles and Adults: Rattan et al. surveyed 735 White Americans (658 in the final sample), and changing a single word in a case description, from “white” to “black” male, made participants see juveniles in general as more similar to adults in blameworthiness and more supportive of life without parole. This connects to my research questions 1 and 2 and my potential question 4 about how perceptions relate to sentencing expectations

The dataset is Redistricting Data Hub Counterfactual Prisoner Adjusted Redistricting Data. It is stored in the projects/rae/data folder, alongside relevant demographic, election, and prison location datasets taken from Dave’s Redistricting App.



My initial research question is very specific “Would prisoner reallocation have changed the distribution of possible legal maps and therefore partisan outcomes in Texas during the 2020 redistricting cycle?” This question is motivated by research done with a professor in the mathematics department developing a new fairness baseline for redistricting. The analysis below was done to better understand the counterfactual data that I am working with before I conduct my formal analysis which will involve using the GerryChain package to sample from the universe of possible maps.

title: Research Plan
text:
Personal Motivation
Write about 100 words about your motivation for undertaking this topic. Why are you personally interested in this material? You can be as personal or as general as you wish here, but this section is about YOUR interest in the material
I’m currently researching partisan gerrymandering and helping a professor in the mathematics department develop a new baseline against which to judge fair redistricting, with a focus on preserving minority-majority districts. I’ve been interested in this topic since I discovered Dr. Wes Pedgen’s research using Markov Chain Monte Carlo for redistricting, as it was the first time I really understood that my passions for math, computers, and government/political science could intersect. Since then, I’ve followed the work of Moon Duchin, who works out of UChicago’s Data and Democracy lab on some of the more advanced models for fair redistricting. I chose Texas as my region of interest since Texas is a state with a large penal population, many districts, and a large Latino population whose interests must be protected under the Voting Rights Act during redistricting. Furthermore, I lived in Dallas this summer!

title: Research Plan
text:
Broader Relevance
Write about 100 words discussing why you think the answers to these questions might matter to others. Is this an understudied topic? Have the conclusions you’ve been seeing about it been wrong or missing something? This is your answer to the “so what?” question
Gerrymandering is a topic that has gotten an increasingly large amount of attention in recent years; however, it appears that academic research on prison gerrymandering has not kept pace, with most well-cited articles on the topic dating back at least four years, if not more. This is unfortunate since prison gerrymandering, just like other kinds of gerrymandering, disproportionately impacts black and brown voters and shifts power from urban centers to rural areas. These effects compound the existing voter suppression and disengagement that is prevalent in communities with high incarceration rates. Prison gerrymandering also violates the “One person, one vote” tenet. In one region, a representative won with just two write-in votes (one of whom was his wife) because only 58 of the over 1300 individuals assigned to his district were part of the non-incarcerated and therefore eligible voting population. The Census Bureau is aware of prison gerrymandering as a pressing issue, as, during the 2020 census process, over 77,000 comments were submitted asking it to reconsider the way it assigns imprisoned individuals to home addresses, with only 4 comments advocating for the current allocation scheme. So this is clearly a topic on which the public has an opinion, yet academic research and government action lag behind.

title: Research Plan
text:
Example Projects
Link to three example projects that are related to your questions or how you’d like to display your results. List them like so:
Alarm Redistricting Project: Since I want to look at the universe of possible maps, why not have users create there own? However, instead of attempting to simply crack or pack districts in a state, users will also be able to view information about imprisoned populations within the state and attempt to gerrymander given this additional information.
Matt Gerken Built Environment Map Tool: I like the idea of a sliding horizontal bar. One side could reveal a map as it currently appears, another could be the “average” map that could occur if PG was rectified or banned.
MCMC On a 7x7 Grid: I like the simulation within “Gridlandia” and the idea that users can modify the partisan makeup and district boundaries. Here, perhaps users could also modify the prison population within each cell of the grid and then generate the distribution of possible partisan outcomes.

title: Research Plan
text:
Relevant Literature
Build a ten item literature review for work related to your questions.
As you consider which 10 to include, try to satisfy these criteria:

1 - 2 written by someone on the inside or system impacted
3ish non-academic sources
at least 5 academic sources
no more than 2 items that we’ve discussed in class / from the syllabus

No need to include a full citation. Instead, list them:
Shifting Power: The Impact of Incarceration on Political Representation: This article looks at how prison gerrymandering shifts power from urban to suburban and rural areas as well as dilutes the vote of minority/black and brown voters. It gives an idea not just of what prison gerrymandering is, but precisely who benefits. It inspired my third research question around queer folks and redistricting.
Redistricting and Incarceration: Examining the Electoral Consequences of New York’s Prohibition on Prison Gerrymandering: This article is interesting because it doesn’t use hypothetical or counterfactual data, but actual maps drawn before and after NYS’s ban on PG. It also focuses more on partisan impacts than other articles, concluding that prison gerrymandering does have partisan consequences.
The Strategic Use of Prisons in Partisan Gerrymandering: This article provides the best description of the mechanism by which PG can be used to create partisan advantages. Whereas other articles highlight empirical number crunching and descriptive analysis, this article acknowledges parties’ agency, asking not just how PG leads to partisan impacts but how parties use PG to gain an advantage.
The End of Prison Gerrymandering: Has Illinois Done Enough to End Prison Gerrymandering by 2030?: This is a great resource with a background on the beginning of mass incarceration, the history of prison gerrymandering, and its current legacy/effects.
Final 2020 Census Residence Criteria and Residence Situations: This is an overview of the comments the Census Bureau received about its “usual residence” (UR) definition ahead of the 2020 census. The comments overwhelmingly support changing the definition of UR to allow prisoners to be assigned to their home neighborhoods and give an overview of the main arguments against prison gerrymandering. This gives me background on public perception/opinion regarding the UR definition and further background on the harm caused by the current UR criteria. This was as close as I could find to “lived experience” or unpolished commentary on prison gerrymandering, unfortunately.
ReCom: A family of Markov Chains for Redistricting: This is the paper introducing Moon Duchin’s ReCom ensemble which is one way to sample from the distribution of existing maps. It also provides some overview of ensembles (so called flip chains) and current model’s drawbacks. It provides theoretical grounding for answering Q2.
Incarcerate LGBTQ+ Adults and Youth: Incarcerated-LGBTQ-Youth-and-Adults.pdf This gives an overview of the LGBTQ+ prison population: who they are, why they are incarcerated at higher rates, and the common issues they face inside. It also presents potential reforms for decreasing the queer incarcerated population. Though it doesn’t directly connect to a research question, it gives a broad overview of the population of interest for Q3.
States were incredibly successful at reallocating incarcerated people to their home addresses in 2020: A review of the data: This article discusses the current limitations of reallocating individuals to their home addresses and examines how successful states were. Two limits were the presence of federal prisons and arbitrary limitations on reallocation by states, which may be useful if I decide to take a counterfactual approach to answering my research question.
Prison Gerrymandering”: How much do prison population counts matter for redistricting outcomes?: This article essentially takes the approach that I am interested in using, but with a different sampling algorithm and using NY 2010 redistricting data. I am interested in using 2020 data (or 2030 projection data) in Texas, but my methods and limitations will largely be similar. I did not know this study existed when I was crafting my initial research question so any similarity is coincidental.
One area of future work mentioned in this article is to simulate higher incarceration numbers for NYS on which to repeat the methodology. This, in part, motivates my use of Texas as a case study in my research, since Texas has an incarceration rate doubling NY’s, so may give insight into PG dynamics within high-incarceration states.
Sequential Monte Carlo for sampling balanced and compact redistricting plans: This is the paper that introduced the sampling method used in the previous paper. Though I am most familiar with Moon Duchin’s Recom method, I am interested in learning more about other sampling methods that could be useful in my analysis.
Prison Gerrymandering in Texas: Distorting Political Representation and Exacerbating Racial Disparities: This is a very recent article about Texas’ prison gerrymandering. It delineates the harms that prison gerrymandering may lead to in Texas, and it serves to motivate my focus on the state of Texas, which currently has no laws banning PG.

title: Ensemble analysis of prison gerrymandering refroms
text: Current methods in detecting partisan gerrymandering revolve around the use of ensemble models, which sample from the universe of possible legal maps in order to better understand the distribution of these maps and whether proposed maps are within the range of possibility if no partisan intent is assumed. However, ensembles are rarely used in any studies of prison gerrymandering and its effect, and I wonder whether ensembles, specifically Dr. Moon Duchin’s Recombination (ReCom) or Reversible Recombination models (RevReCom), have untapped utility in this context. First, I intend to examine whether the distribution of Democratic seats won across possible legal maps in Texas changes measurably after the reallocation of incarcerated Texans to their last known home address. Second, I’m interested in not only quantifying the impact of reallocation on the possible realm of maps, but investigating a way to use pre-allocation ensembles to detect the presence of prison gerrymandering. I choose to focus on Texas due to its relevance in the literature.

What most surprised you about the data you’ve been working with? I am curious and should have probably expanded on my poverty question and calculated the proportion of victims and suspects who were white in areas marked as having a high poverty rate, as poverty is so racialized (associated with people of color, especially Black and brown) and so I wonder if the reports of domestic violence for the white people in the dataset have anything to do with poverty levels.
What questions do you still have? What would help you answer them? I still do not have information/data on how prosecution is conducted regarding domestic violence cases, and it’s already hard to tell if there is bias involved in the incident report data, let alone in the entire justice process. I definitely still think the dataset I have is useful in identifying the general demographic (race & sex), geographical, and socioeconomic circumstances that most often come into contact with the police, but I want to find supplemental data that deals more explicitly with arrests and convictions, as this dataset only aggregates all the incident reports, which from my understanding may or may not have resulted in an arrest.

How has your thinking changed since you first wrote your research question? I definitely feel like I need to find more population data to be able to work more with my main dataset and thus answer my research question more effectively. It has also proven kind of difficult to find straightforward data about potential racial bias in criminal courts specifically, as in I have not gotten arrest or conviction data that has included the defendant and the plaintiff’s racial demographics yet. title: Influence of Race on Domestic Violence Arrests and Convictions
text:
My research question will address the issue of whether or not race plays a role in the rate of domestic violence-related arrests and the length and/or severity of charges, and if so in what ways/to what extent is it indicative of a broader pattern of racial discrimination within US criminal courts and legal decision-making? I will provide background for my topic by identifying the legal frameworks surrounding what constitutes domestic violence in criminal law, and then I will try to find relevant demographic data for arrests and convictions in domestic violence crimes to identify what role race may play in justice decisions for these crimes and in what specific ways this bias manifests. I will also be extending my analysis to examine whether or not sex and socioeconomic status (as measured by poverty/unemployment) serve as confounding factors or otherwise moderate the role of racial bias in the prosecution of domestic violence.

title: Geography Cluster Working Document
text:
Stage #1 Reflection
The overarching theme of our group is the cause and effect of prisons and their geography. Collectively we took an interest in things such as gerrymandering, regional differences, how the location of correctional facilities impact the surrounding area, and how geography impacts the school environments of young adults. Across Rae and Jessie’s work rural towns and economies are especially relevant; prison gerrymandering typically shifts representation from urban areas to rural settings, which is due to the placement of prisons in primarily rural areas; such placement is within the scope of Jessie’s investigation. Hayden and Kayla both plan to look at how geographical differences can impact how individuals interact with the legal system. In short, Jessie will investigate why a prison is placed where it is, Rae will look at the state and national political implications of that placement, Hayden will explore how school/neighborhood segregation impacts juveniles, and Kayla narrows that down into examining the effects on how, specifically, Black individuals are treated within the legal system through regional differences.
We’ve started to compile a list of relevant pieces of literature to our topics and have already started to see certain overlaps. We’re hoping that these similarities will also be helpful when it comes to looking for datasets. Kayla and Hayden are both taking a comparative approach by looking at regional differences. While Hayden is looking at a smaller scale of just Mecklenburg County and Kalya at the general “North” and “South”, the overlap in investigating how a person’s place can impact their outcomes will be a shared theme. One general theme will be the idea of representation, which is a highly social concept, with far reaching societal impacts, so we hope that we can all help capture this more humanistic side together. Rae and Jessie may both rely on datasets relating to the geographic location of correctional facilities. Hayden and Rae will also likely both be looking at how people are geographically dispersed both demographically and socioeconomically. We all hope that we can use this research cluster as a way to bounce ideas off of each other despite there being differences between our projects. Having a general idea of what each of us is working on will be helpful as we’ll be able to see how each other’s projects progress and the background that surrounds them.

title: Stage 2 Writing
text:
What data did you think you’d find that you weren’t able to find?
Before starting this project, I was unsure if I would be able to find the kind of crime data I needed for Washington state counties beyond just general crime statistics. After making a request for data from the Washington Association of Sheriffs and Police Chiefs, I was able to obtain a list of all logged offenses in Washington 2020-2025. Having a list of every single specific offense allowed me to divide the offenses into violent offenses and other offenses. Initially, I just just thinking about crime generally, but having this specific data has allowed me to add a dimension to my project: the relationship of law enforcement and social spending on violent crime rates specifically.


What most surprised you about the data you’ve been working with?
I was surprised to learn that social services spending is a lot higher than law enforcement spending, on average. In my Stage 2 work, I found that in 2025, Washington counties spent an average of $24,960,060 on law enforcement and $65,967,350 on social services. This challenged my initial assumptions about the allocation of resources in the state.


What questions do you still have? What would help you answer them?
I want to compare data across years. I have crime data from 2020-2025 and I could obtain spending data within this range. I have the tools I need to make this comparison, I just need to think about how I will go about it. Using even just one other year makes my questions more interesting because it changes from an exploration of if more spending in one category is associated with less (or more) crime to if a change in spending in one category is associated with a change in crime rates. In the next stage of the project, I plan to use 2024 data alongside the 2025 data I’ve already been working with to highlight any meaningful changes in spending or crime that have occurred.
Further, I want to evaluate the statistical significance of my findings. I also want to think about other variables that I’m not working with that may be influencing my findings.


What story are you trying to tell with this data?
I am interested in creating a project that examines how counties’ priorities and resource allocation relate to the conditions that communities experience. Law enforcement and social spending reflect different approaches to public safety, and examining these alongside crime rates can (hopefully) reveal whether spending in either area can actually be associated with safer communities. I am also thinking about resource allocation from an economic efficiency standpoint. What if a reallocation of resources can lower crime at the same cost? My project can’t answer this question, but my work could use evidence from Washington counties to hypothesize that a greater investment in one spending area could lower crime.


How do you think the insights you’re discovering will be best presented? That is, what kinds of displays might be most effective for the story you’re trying to tell?
In Stage 2, I created some basic scatterplots with lines of best fit to show the relationships between crime rates and per capita spending. I think this is a simple and effective way of demonstrating the relationships between my variables. My scatterplots did have some major outliers which I think would be helpful to label. I think it would be interesting to further research these specific points and find information that could explain why these points land so far from the general trend.

title: Washington State Law Enforcement & Social Spending
text:
This project explores the breakdown of police spending and social spending in each of Washington state’s 39 counties. Using Washington state fiscal information, I am looking at each county’s budget to see which counties spend the most on social services relative to their police spending. Further, I am looking at crime statistics by county to explore the relationship between police spending, social spending, and crime. Because some studies have shown that police spending reduces crime short-term while social spending reduces crime long-term, I am going to identify any significant changes in a county’s police or social spending, then evaluate the impact of these changes on crime after a given period.

title: SDS316 Syllabus
text:
Prerequisites: SDS 270 or SDS 271 or CSC 210 or CSC/SDS 235 or by permission of the instructor
Meetings: Monday & Wednesday || 7:00 - 8:15pm || Bass 002
💡 Office hours, booking non-office hour time, etc You can also catch me for about 20 minutes after class on Wednesdays.


The United States criminal legal system is increasingly data-driven. Technologies like recidivism algorithms and predictive policing give the appearance of numerical objectivity. But, without sufficient context, we cannot understand how these technologies work or the data that they are using. This course introduces students to the theory and practice of handling data about the United States criminal legal system. Students will engage with this material through in-depth reading about the history of crime, policing, and incarceration; seminar discussions; research design; and large data-driven projects.



After completing this course, students will be able to:

Identify ethical concerns in the development and implementation of data-driven systems, specifically in the context of the criminal legal system

Identify the phases of the US criminal legal system, and several data-centric challenges within each

Design and execute a data-centered research project about the criminal legal system

Implement a data-driven dashboard to showcase their findings

Convey quantitative information in written, oral and graphical forms of communication to both technical and nontechnical audiences (an SDS learning objective)

title: SDS316 Syllabus
text:
Participation and Classroom Expectations
When we have classroom discussions, we’ll be covering material that may have impacted our lives or our communities. It is impossible to separate our lived experience from our academic work, and indeed our expertise and knowledge lies within our experiences. That’s an academic way of saying – bring your whole self to class with you because it’s who you are and because it makes you a better student and researcher. When everyone is bringing their whole selves to class, there is likely to be disagreement, conflict, or at least some discomfort. During the first week of class, we’ll set some norms together that work for our group.
I expect that you will come to class prepared to participate, and willing to participate in ways that are both familiar and unfamiliar to you.

Names and Personal Pronouns
I affirm all forms of gender expression and identities. If you prefer to be called a different name than what is on the class roster, please let me know. Feel free to correct me on your gender pronoun, if you don’t use any pronouns, or if your pronouns change during the semester. If you have any questions or concerns about being addressed respectfully, please do not hesitate to contact me. For more information, see Smith’s page about gender identity and expression.


Time Commitment and Labor Expectations
This course requires a weekly time commitment. On an average week, you’ll spend about 10-12 hours total on this course (this is also a federal requirement for universities!). In a typical week, you’ll spend 2.5 in class, about 3 hours doing reading, and an average of 4-6 hours working on class projects. The distribution of this time will shift over the course of the semester with some weeks having mostly reading work and others having mostly hands-on development work.


Office Hours
My office hours are listed in the document linked from the syllabus, and I strongly encourage each of you to use them. Studies have shown (e.g. Henry, 2014) that some students do not take advantage of office hours or are otherwise afraid to “bother” faculty. When I was an undergraduate student, the first in my family to go to college, I never went to office hours and I really missed out. This paragraph is my formal invitation to you to come to as many office hours as are helpful to you. Holding these hours is a literal part of my job – and I like my job – so please use all of the resources available to you, including my office hours.

title: SDS316 Syllabus
text:
Course Policies

Code of Conduct and Interpersonal Safety
It is important to me to create a classroom environment where everyone can be successful. We will work together to develop a classroom code of conduct that works for the group that we will become this semester, and we will check in about it regularly. At a minimum, this code of conduct will include:

respecting and affirming the identities and lived experiences of everyone in the classroom

moving slowly when difficult content is presented

during disagreements, disagreeing with the idea and not the person

assuming positive intent when someone makes a mistake

honoring those who speak up about something that doesn’t feel good

This class has an unconditional timeout policy, which means that any person can call a time out for any reason. When someone calls a time out, we will thank them for being brave enough to assert their needs. My commitment to you is that I will:

work to acknowledge structural and interpersonal power imbalances
believe your accounts of your life and experiences
interrupt any harassing behavior

If you have any concerns or suggestions for how to make this class more inclusive, please reach out to me. If you’d rather do it anonymously, please leave a note in my faculty mailbox in Burton Hall.


Attendance
You are an adult and you can choose whether or not to attend class. Except in exceptional circumstances, I don’t provide summaries of missed material for students who miss class; students who miss class will need to get course materials from a classmate.
If you are sick, please don’t come to class! In general, the SDS department has a no-remote-attendance policy. However, we live in community here, and staying home from class when you’re sick is a way of caring for your Smith community. In these cases, you are welcome to contact a classmate to zoom you into class. I will not set up zoom for you when you are sick. Students should reach out to their class dean in the event of an extended illness or emergency; they can help you to navigate these situations with your instructors. Consistent with the college’s policy on student academic standing, if you miss more than four weeks of class meetings, you are in danger of failing to earn credit for this course (receiving a grade of E).


Electronic Devices
This course combines seminar-style discussion and hands-on technical work.
During seminar conversations, I ask that you close your laptops, put away your phones and participate in class discussion. Of course, there may be times when you need to take a call or send a message. In these cases, please step out of class to do so – do not use your device under the table, out of respect for your classmates. The is no exception to this policy other than an ARC accommodation.
During lab work, I expect you to come to class with a working development environment – there will not be time to troubleshoot your machine in class. If you need help, please come to office hours.


AI Policy
This Fall 2026 edition of the class will have a pedagogical partner who will join us to think about if and how we use AI in this class. The policy is one we will develop together. However, there are some guideliness that will hold regardless of the outcome of that partnership:

you may not use AI to generate ideas. AI is not an idea generation machine, it is a probablistic language predictor. As a result, any idea that AI generates is one that many people have had before.

you may not use AI to generate writing or to edit/proofread something that you wrote. I would rather read your worst writing on your worst day than a single sentence generated by AI. Communicating complex ideas of the key skills that we practice in this class and AI cannot help you develop that skill, unfortunately.

title: Coding Inequality, Algorithms, Legality, and the end!
text:
Reading
Chapter 6:

Feedback loops, an increase in policing produces more recorded incidents → which tends to justify further surveillance in certain communities → and loop continues
Self-fulfilling statistical prophecies, quantified practices often exacerbate inequalities in stop patterns, creating arrest statistics needed to justify stereotypes (confirmation bias)
Data codifies a secondary surveillance network and widens the criminal justice dragnet unequally
System avoidance, people may avoid becoming visible to the criminal legal system by avoiding public services, often disproportionately affecting marginalized communities

title: Coding Inequality, Algorithms, Legality, and the end!
text:
Continued…
Chapter 7 + 8:

Fourth amendment, big data complicates these protections as police can develop suspicion in ways that challenge traditional ideas (parallel construction)
Legal protections lag behind technology
Community engagement and accountability, big data is a social and institutional issue not just a technological one, so transparency, oversight, and public participation are important in evaluating surveillance systems
Six provocations: Slow down, police the police, identify and remediate errors, direct nonpunitive interventions, clear cases and solve cold ones, redefine successful policing

title: Coding Inequality, Algorithms, Legality, and the end!
text:
Main Points

“If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear… however, the legitimacy of using a series of data points to reconstruct an individual’s intentions and behaviors – whether incriminating or exculpatory – and using that data to predict future behaviors, relies on the fallibility of both the state and the state actors who enter data.” (pg. 112) INTENTION
“Existing research underestimates the effects of involvement in the criminal justice system when that involvement is tied to impenetrable, interwoven, and proprietary data systems. We literally don’t know where all the data goes.” (pg. 141) SIZE
