*Discusses the systemic racism present in the US. “According to a 2017 report, Black men got 19.1% longer sentences for the same federal crime than white men between 2012-2016.” “Despite making up just 13% of the US population, Black people make up 38% of the population in jails and prisons.”

title: Historical Significance, Carceral Space, Racial Criminalization
text:
Reading
Introduction - Set a historical significance of growing data, data collection has always been politically motivated - Creation of social datasets assists in the social heirarchy those in charge are trying to promote

title: Historical Significance, Carceral Space, Racial Criminalization
text:
Continued…
Chapter 1 - Data collection and analysis has always been to ostrosize the “inferior” racial group at the time, Irish, Italian, German, then Black people - Datasets including race were the catalist of grouping all of the hated European Immigrants into the white catagory, making the outliers the black category - Trying to explain crime as a social construct paved the way for ignoring physcial and only focusing on social demographics - More data means more reason to patrol

title: Historical Significance, Carceral Space, Racial Criminalization
text:
Main Points

“As such, computational criminology is incapable of grasping internal differentiations within the classes of offenders it tabulates. No distinctions are made between the individual who sells narcotics to support a family and the individual who sells them for a gun cartel in computational criminology’s system of reference, yet both are coded as targets for heightened police scrutiny.” (pg. 55) LOSS OF IDENTITY
“From the start, the social function of computational criminology was to produce targets for patrol forces; it is one-dimensional thought operating in two-dimensional space.” (pg. 53) EFFICIENCY

title: Historical Significance, Carceral Space, Racial Criminalization
text:
Questions!

Where do we go from here in order to break the self fulfilling prophecy of systemic racism, what can change about how we collect data and police to stop contributing to the problem?
Does collecting demographic data actually help, or does it contribute to putting people into boxes? What are examples of positive and negative uses of demographic data collection?

Chicago Paid $2.7M for System Designed to Flag Officers With Multiple Complaints

This article highlights a tension Jefferson explores in this chapter about what happens when these types of systems are used on officers.

title: A Fully Automated Police Apparatus
text:
Main Points
Historical context of police digitization

Economic inequality increased in NYC and Chicago in the 80s and 90s: increases in unemployment and crime
Responses to crime were motivated by capital losses: crime hurt businesses and lowered property values
Predictive policing software amplified the disproportionate targeting of Black and Hispanic individuals; technological advances legitimized the existing patterns of racialized policing

title: A Fully Automated Police Apparatus
text:
NYC

1994: Clinton’s Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act
Massive use of tax dollars integrating IT with the police
Giuliani-era reform: zero-tolerance policing & broken windows theory
CompStat created to identify crime hotspots and governmentalize police behavior
Impact zoning deployed officers to hotspots

title: A Fully Automated Police Apparatus
text:
Chicago

Gang violence was compared to the Colombian drug war to lobby for military technology
Oracle Corporation created the CLEAR (Citizen Law Enforcement Analysis and Reporting) system, a database that produced targets for patrol units
Deployment Operations Center (DOC): a software that generated targets for patrol units and tried to predict future offenses
CLEAR & DOC used to rationalize uneven distributions of patrol units

title: A Fully Automated Police Apparatus
text:
Questions

“the city found itself confronted with the problem of populations whose hindrance on profit rates was increasing” (111). Jefferson argues that under capitalism, policing serves to protect economic interests rather than promote public safety. How do economic interests shape which behaviors/actions are criminalized and who is targeted by the police?
“predictive policing identifies entire demographics and neighborhoods as criminally predisposed” (128). How might predictive policing create a self-fulfilling prophecy?
“an organization’s turn to data analytics increases its demand for additional data” (116). Does the demand for more data ever end? How does this demand contribute to the expansion of surveillance, and will the expansion of surveillance ever end?

title: Virtual Environments
text:
First, some vocab:

Python dependency: an external package that a script (or other package requires to run)
Executable: a script that can be read and run by your computer without additional compiling
Interpreter: an executable file that takes a .py script and actually runs it 
symlinks: pointers that lead to a file
PATH executable: the directory in which a computer can search for executables when the full path name isn’t given

title: Virtual Environments
section: Why not just install packages globally?
text:
Why not just install packages globally?

Dependency conflicts! Different projects need different versions of packages (and each package may need a specific version of its dependencies)

title: Virtual Environments
text:
Enter Virtual Environments…
Essentially, a subfolder specific to a single Python version containing all of the executables and packages needed for your project.
Two types we’ll cover today:

Python’s built-in environment manager: venv
uv, modern package installer built in Rust

title: Virtual Environments
text:
Pros of Venv

Built-in (no additional install)
Easy to use and conceptualize

Venv is used largely for dependency isolation.

title: Virtual Environments
section: What happens when you use venv?
text:
What happens when you use venv?
Activating a venv changes where your computer assumes your files are! Here’s what changes:

sys.prefix and sys.exec_prefix:


sys.prefix: path to platform-independent (OS-independent) Python packages
sys.exec_prefix: path to platform-dependent (OS-ndependent) Python packages

title: Virtual Environments
section: What happens when you use venv (cont.)
text:
What happens when you use venv (cont.)

PYTHONPATH:


tells Python where to look for modules (i.e., to go to venv sites-packaes NOT the base sites-packages)


PATH variable changes


modifies the PATH variable to include the virtual environment Python executable

In short: Python is told to STOP looking for exectuables, modules, and 3rd-party packages in the directory where base Python is installed. Instead, Python looks for files inside the virtual environment

title: Virtual Environments
text:
What does a “venv” include?

A typical virtual environment file setup
/bin: stores the python interpreter, pip, and activation symlinks
lib/sites-packages: directory where 3rd party packages are installed
/include directory where C headers for packages are stored
Configuration file: all details needed to configure the venv

title: Virtual Environments
text:
What about uv?

faster package installation than venv/pip install
more robust dependency handling
project initialization (will initialize a root directory, git repo, .gitignore, etc.)

title: Virtual Environments
text:
What does uv include?

A uv project file setup for a project called “rpcats”Here the .toml file is a configuration file!

title: Virtual Environments
text:
In conclusion…

always use some kind of virtual environment / project isolation method
use venv for “simple and dirty”
use uv for more complex projects that involve publishing or development

Main Points

title: Directed Surveillance and Police Pushback
text:
Questions?
“Operation LASER was not simply about removing violent offenders with “laser like precision”, it was also functioning to justify mass intelligence gathering and functioning as a deterrent, signaling to people that they’re being tracked by law enforcement”(78).

We’ve had a similar conversation about the justification of big data. At what level does data collection cross the line and is no longer justifiable?

Brayne discusses friction in the form of an “us vs them” mentality between many different groups (e.g. officers vs employees). Did any of them surprise you?
One of the captains compared the rate of crime to unemployment rates, and how there is a point of “friction”. He then said that after that, you need to innovate. Brayne notes that “innovating has increasingly meant more data[…]” (58-59)

Does innovating have to mean more data? What other innovative strategies are there to lower crime?
